What We Do

"Connecting Decision makers to change makers"

Simphiwe Mtetwa is a trusted platform for influence and impact, strategically connecting South Africa's foremost decision-makers with the changemakers driving meaningful progress. As Africa's leading source for Corporate Social Investment (CSI) intelligence, we deliver well-researched, forward-thinking content; produce professionally designed CSI reports for corporates, NGOs and foundations; convene high-level, results-driven events; and encourage fresh perspectives that challenge conventional thinking.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best Corporate

Oceana Group: Empowering Small-Scale Fishing Communities for a Sustainable Future

CSI Legacy Awards · Honouree Feature

Category

Best Corporate

Honouree

Oceana Group

Recognised

2026

All Winners

For more than 100 years, Oceana Group has been a cornerstone of Africa's fishing industry, building a reputation for quality, innovation and responsible business. Today, the company is equally recognised for its commitment to creating sustainable social impact, having been honoured with the CSI Legacy Award for Best Corporate. The award acknowledges organisations that demonstrate exceptional leadership in corporate social investment through initiatives that deliver measurable, lasting benefits to communities.

Central to Oceana's award-winning approach is Cooperative Sense, a pioneering programme that empowers South Africa's small-scale fishing communities. While these communities play a vital role in the country's food security and coastal economy, they often face significant challenges, including limited access to formal training, financial management skills, cooperative governance support, sea safety education and market opportunities.

Recognising these barriers, Oceana developed Cooperative Sense in partnership with the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) and the National Sea Rescue Institute (NSRI). The programme provides practical, NQF-accredited training through the Oceana Maritime Academy, equipping participants with the skills and confidence to build stronger, more sustainable fishing cooperatives.

The curriculum combines financial literacy, cooperative governance, sustainable fishing practices and sea safety training, ensuring participants are better prepared to manage both the business and operational aspects of their work. Beyond improving livelihoods, the programme also promotes environmental stewardship by encouraging responsible fishing practices that help protect South Africa's valuable marine resources for future generations.

The impact of Cooperative Sense has been both measurable and inspiring. More than 95% of participants reported an improvement in their financial literacy, enabling them to make better financial decisions for themselves and their cooperatives. Nearly 89% gained critical emergency response and sea safety skills, significantly improving their preparedness while working in often hazardous marine environments. Supported by an investment of more than R5 million, the programme has become a scalable model for community development that combines economic empowerment with environmental sustainability and improved safety.

Oceana's commitment to social impact extends well beyond the fishing industry. Through its broader corporate social investment initiatives, the Group has also made a significant contribution to addressing food insecurity across South Africa. By providing more than one million meals to vulnerable households, Oceana has helped improve nutrition and support communities facing hardship, reinforcing its belief that business success should translate into tangible social value.

What distinguishes Oceana's approach is its focus on long-term empowerment rather than short-term assistance. By investing in education, skills development and capacity building, the company is helping create resilient communities that are better equipped to generate sustainable incomes, strengthen local economies and preserve marine ecosystems. Its collaborative partnerships with government and civil society organisations further demonstrate the power of collective action in addressing complex social and environmental challenges.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best Corporate is a fitting recognition of Oceana Group's unwavering commitment to creating shared value. The award celebrates not only the measurable success of Cooperative Sense but also the company's broader vision of responsible corporate citizenship—one that places people, partnerships and sustainability at the centre of its business strategy.

As South Africa continues to navigate economic and environmental challenges, Oceana Group stands as an example of how corporate social investment can create meaningful, lasting change. By empowering small-scale fishing communities, improving food security and investing in sustainable livelihoods, Oceana is ensuring that its legacy extends far beyond the ocean—creating stronger communities and a more resilient future for generations to come.

About the CSI Legacy Awards

The CSI Legacy Awards is a best-practice programme that enables players in the South African CSI industry to learn from one another. In each category, programmes that have had the most positive impact on communities across the country are recognised and celebrated.

Entrants are judged by a cohort of industry experts who are unaware of the identities of the entrants — ensuring recognition is earned on merit alone.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best CEO

Martin Sweet: Bringing Theatres of Learning to 1.6 Million Young South Africans

Primestars South Africa · Honouree Feature

Category

Best CEO

Honouree

Martin Sweet

Organisation

Primestars South Africa

Recognised

2026

All Winners

For more than two decades, Martin Sweet, Founder and Executive Chairman of Primestars South Africa, has dedicated his career to ensuring that every young South African has the opportunity to realise their full potential, regardless of their background or circumstances. His visionary leadership and unwavering commitment to educational equity have earned him the CSI Legacy Award for Best CEO, recognising his exceptional contribution to corporate social investment and his enduring impact on the lives of more than 1.6 million young people across South Africa.

Established over 21 years ago, Primestars South Africa was founded on a simple but powerful belief: that a child's postcode should never determine the quality of education, opportunities or future they can access. Under Martin Sweet's leadership, the organisation has become one of South Africa's most innovative youth development organisations, delivering transformative educational programmes to learners in under-resourced communities across all nine provinces.

At the heart of Primestars' success is its pioneering Theatres of Learning model. Recognising that many schools lack the infrastructure and resources to provide engaging educational experiences, the organisation uses both conventional and mobile cinemas to bring immersive learning directly into communities. These interactive sessions are supported by learner workbooks, mentorship opportunities and structured follow-up programmes that reinforce key lessons and encourage practical application beyond the classroom.

This innovative approach has enabled Primestars to engage learners in ways that are both accessible and memorable, creating meaningful educational experiences that inspire confidence, broaden horizons and encourage lifelong learning. More importantly, it has demonstrated how creativity and innovation can overcome barriers to education and create opportunities at scale.

Under Sweet's leadership, Primestars has developed a diverse portfolio of programmes that address the multiple challenges facing South Africa's youth. eduCate, one of the organisation's flagship initiatives, provides CAPS-aligned Mathematics and Science revision support ahead of matric examinations, helping learners improve academic performance while opening pathways into science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) careers.

Recognising the importance of economic participation, Step Up 2 A Start Up equips young people with entrepreneurial skills linked to the green economy, encouraging innovation while preparing participants for emerging employment opportunities. Through practical learning experiences, the programme empowers learners to become job creators rather than job seekers.

Primestars has also taken a proactive role in addressing some of South Africa's most pressing social challenges. What About The Boys? encourages boys and young men to explore concepts of empathy, accountability and respectful relationships, contributing to broader efforts to prevent gender-based violence by addressing harmful attitudes before they become entrenched.

Financial capability is another critical pillar of the organisation's work. Through Rethink Rands, learners gain practical financial literacy skills that enable them to make informed decisions about saving, budgeting and responsible money management. Meanwhile, the Future Leaders Challenge nurtures servant leadership, ethical decision-making and active citizenship, inspiring young people to become positive role models within their schools and communities.

Career guidance initiatives further strengthen Primestars' holistic approach by connecting learners with industry professionals and exposing them to a wide range of career opportunities, helping bridge the gap between education and employment.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best CEO is a fitting tribute to Martin Sweet's visionary leadership and his steadfast belief that education remains one of the most powerful tools for social transformation. Rather than simply delivering programmes, he has built an organisation that continuously adapts to meet the evolving needs of South Africa's youth while maintaining a relentless focus on measurable impact.

Today, Primestars South Africa stands as a testament to what purpose-driven leadership can achieve. Through innovation, collaboration and an unwavering commitment to creating opportunities, Martin Sweet has transformed the lives of more than 1.6 million young people and inspired countless others to believe that their circumstances need not define their future. His legacy is measured not only by the programmes he has created, but by the generations of confident, capable and empowered young South Africans who are shaping a brighter future for themselves, their communities and the country.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best Woman in CSI

Juanita Pardesi: Building Dignity Through Community-Led Development

Seriti Institute · Honouree Feature

Category

Best Woman in CSI

Honouree

Juanita Pardesi

Organisation

Seriti Institute

Recognised

2026

All Winners

For more than 15 years, Juanita Pardesi, Chief Executive Officer of Seriti Institute, has championed a vision of development that places people, dignity and opportunity at its centre. Her unwavering commitment to creating sustainable livelihoods and empowering communities has earned her the CSI Legacy Award for Best Woman in CSI, recognising her outstanding leadership and transformative contribution to social impact in South Africa.

Since the founding of Seriti Institute in 2009, the organisation has become one of the country's leading community development organisations, operating across all nine provinces and creating more than 16,000 work opportunities. Under Pardesi's leadership, Seriti has demonstrated that lasting change is achieved not through charity, but by equipping communities with the skills, resources and opportunities they need to shape their own futures.

When Juanita Pardesi assumed leadership of Seriti Institute, the organisation was facing significant challenges and was close to closure. Through a combination of strategic vision, collaborative leadership and an unwavering belief in community-driven development, she transformed Seriti into a nationally recognised, youth-focused organisation that works at the intersection of civil society, business and government. Today, the Institute develops innovative solutions that address unemployment, food insecurity, inequality and climate resilience, while ensuring that communities remain active participants in designing and delivering those solutions.

The initiative that formed the basis of Seriti's recognition at the CSI Legacy Awards is the Deelpan Multi-Functional Agri-Node (MFAN) in South Africa's North West Province. Situated in a rural community with limited economic opportunities, the project demonstrates how integrated, community-led development can create lasting economic and social transformation.

Rather than introducing short-term interventions, Seriti worked alongside local residents to establish Deelpan as a vibrant centre for food production, enterprise development and green livelihoods. Through strategic partnerships with the National Youth Service and the Social Employment Fund, the initiative has supported more than 1,700 community members over a three-year period, creating meaningful work while strengthening local food systems and economic resilience.

At the heart of the MFAN model is an integrated approach that combines agroecology training, enterprise development and market access. Participants receive practical agricultural training while also developing the business skills needed to build sustainable enterprises. Smallholder farmers produce fresh fruit and vegetables that are sold locally through the Community Fresh App, creating a reliable, community-based supply chain that benefits both producers and consumers.

This approach not only generates income but also strengthens food security within the community, reduces dependency on external food sources and promotes environmentally sustainable farming practices. By prioritising agroecology and climate-smart agriculture, the programme equips participants with the knowledge to adapt to changing environmental conditions while protecting natural resources for future generations.

A defining feature of the initiative is its focus on empowering young people and women, groups that often experience the greatest barriers to employment and economic participation. By providing practical skills, work experience and entrepreneurial opportunities, the programme enables participants to build sustainable livelihoods while contributing to the long-term prosperity of their communities.

The success of the Deelpan MFAN has demonstrated the potential of community-led development to address multiple social challenges simultaneously. As a result, the model is now being replicated in other provinces, extending its impact and providing a scalable blueprint for inclusive rural development across South Africa.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best Woman in CSI is a fitting recognition of Juanita Pardesi's exceptional leadership and her steadfast belief that dignity is created through meaningful work, not dependence. Throughout her career, she has consistently challenged conventional approaches to development by placing trust in communities and investing in their capacity to lead their own transformation.

Today, Seriti Institute stands as a powerful example of what visionary leadership can achieve when purpose is matched with collaboration and innovation. Through Juanita Pardesi's leadership, thousands of South Africans have gained access to meaningful work, improved food security and sustainable economic opportunities. Her legacy extends far beyond individual projects—it is reflected in stronger communities, empowered local leaders and a development model that continues to inspire lasting change across the country.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best Social Enterprise

Taking Care of Business: Circular Economy, Dignity and Lasting Independence

Taking Care of Business · Honouree Feature

Category

Best Social Enterprise

Honouree

Taking Care of Business

Represented By

Tracey Chambers

Recognised

2026

All Winners

Taking Care of Business (TCB) has been named the recipient of the CSI Legacy Award for Best Social Enterprise, recognising its outstanding contribution to tackling poverty, creating sustainable livelihoods and advancing South Africa's circular economy. Through an innovative model that combines entrepreneurship, environmental sustainability and community development, TCB has demonstrated how social enterprises can deliver lasting social and economic impact while empowering individuals to build independent futures.

Represented by Tracey Chambers, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, Taking Care of Business has become one of South Africa's leading examples of purpose-driven enterprise. For years, the organisation has worked alongside vulnerable communities, supporting thousands of aspiring entrepreneurs—particularly unemployed mothers, women and early childhood development (ECD) practitioners—to establish sustainable businesses that generate long-term income and financial resilience.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best Social Enterprise is a fitting recognition of an organisation that has consistently challenged conventional approaches to poverty alleviation. Rather than providing short-term relief, TCB focuses on equipping people with the skills, resources and opportunities they need to create lasting economic independence while contributing to healthier communities and a more sustainable environment.

At the heart of TCB's success is its integrated development model, which addresses several of South Africa's most pressing social and environmental challenges simultaneously. Through flagship initiatives including Resell, Repair, Remake, Reskill and Grow ECD, the organisation creates pathways to employment and entrepreneurship while reducing waste and promoting responsible resource management.

The Resell programme enables entrepreneurs to generate income by selling quality pre-owned goods, providing affordable products to communities while extending the life cycle of valuable resources. Repair develops technical skills that allow participants to restore and maintain household goods, reducing waste and creating new economic opportunities. Through Remake, discarded materials are transformed into new products, demonstrating the value of innovation within the circular economy and encouraging more sustainable patterns of production and consumption.

Complementing these initiatives, Reskill provides practical business training, entrepreneurial development and financial management skills that equip participants to establish and grow viable enterprises. Recognising the critical role that early childhood education plays in breaking the cycle of poverty, Grow ECD supports practitioners by strengthening the quality and sustainability of early learning centres, improving educational outcomes while creating stable livelihoods for those working within the sector.

Together, these programmes address the interconnected challenges of unemployment, inequality, waste management and limited access to economic opportunities. By providing participants with practical skills, mentorship and ongoing support, TCB enables individuals not only to earn an income but also to build businesses capable of supporting their families and contributing to local economic development.

Under the leadership of Tracey Chambers, a Chartered Accountant and internationally recognised social entrepreneur, Taking Care of Business has developed a model that demonstrates the power of collaboration between the corporate, development and community sectors. Her vision has always been rooted in the belief that empowering women and families creates a ripple effect that strengthens entire communities, and this philosophy continues to guide the organisation's work.

The measurable impact of TCB's programmes is reflected in the thousands of entrepreneurs who have achieved greater financial independence while participating in initiatives that reduce waste, promote recycling and contribute to environmental sustainability. By embedding circular economy principles into every aspect of its work, the organisation has shown that social impact and environmental responsibility are not competing priorities but complementary drivers of sustainable development.

Winning the CSI Legacy Award for Best Social Enterprise celebrates not only Taking Care of Business' impressive achievements to date but also its broader contribution to redefining what social enterprise can accomplish. Its integrated approach proves that lasting solutions to poverty require more than financial assistance—they require opportunity, skills, innovation and dignity.

As South Africa continues to seek inclusive solutions to unemployment, inequality and environmental challenges, Taking Care of Business stands as an inspiring example of how social enterprise can create meaningful, measurable and sustainable change. Through visionary leadership, innovative programmes and an unwavering commitment to empowering people, the organisation is building stronger communities, protecting the environment and creating pathways out of poverty that will benefit generations to come.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best NGO

PinkDrive: Bringing Life-Saving Cancer Screening to the Communities That Need It Most

PinkDrive NPC · Honouree Feature

Category

Best NGO

Honouree

PinkDrive NPC

Founded By

Noelene Kotschan

Recognised

2026

All Winners

PinkDrive NPC has been honoured with the CSI Legacy Award for Best NGO, recognising more than 15 years of unwavering commitment to improving access to life-saving cancer screening, education and early detection services across South Africa. The award celebrates organisations that demonstrate exceptional social impact, innovation and sustainability, and PinkDrive's work has transformed the lives of countless individuals by making preventative healthcare accessible to communities that need it most.

Founded in 2009 by Noelene Kotschan, PinkDrive began with a single mobile mammography unit and a powerful vision: that no one should lose their life to cancer simply because they could not access early screening. Since then, the organisation has grown into South Africa's leading non-profit provider of mobile cancer screening and awareness services, reaching communities across the country through an expanding fleet of mobile healthcare units.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best NGO is a fitting recognition of an organisation that has consistently broken down barriers to healthcare while raising awareness about the importance of early detection. Guided by the belief that early diagnosis saves lives, PinkDrive has built an innovative model that takes healthcare directly to people rather than expecting vulnerable communities to overcome the financial, geographical and social barriers that often prevent them from accessing essential services.

Through its mobile healthcare fleet, PinkDrive delivers a comprehensive range of free screening services to both urban and rural communities. These include clinical breast examinations, mammograms, Pap smears and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) tests, supported by culturally appropriate health education that empowers individuals to recognise early warning signs and seek timely medical care.

For many South Africans, particularly those living in remote or underserved communities, a visit from a PinkDrive mobile unit represents their first opportunity to access preventative healthcare. By bringing diagnostic services directly to communities, the organisation removes some of the most significant obstacles to early detection, including transport costs, long travel distances to healthcare facilities, limited healthcare infrastructure and a lack of awareness about cancer screening.

Beyond delivering clinical services, PinkDrive has become a trusted source of education and advocacy. Its awareness campaigns encourage open conversations about cancer, helping to reduce stigma while promoting the importance of regular screening and early intervention. This educational component has played a critical role in changing health-seeking behaviours, enabling more people to take proactive steps to protect their health.

The organisation's impact is reflected not only in the millions of South Africans it has educated but also in the hundreds of thousands who have received potentially life-saving screenings. For many individuals diagnosed at an early stage, PinkDrive has provided the crucial opportunity for timely treatment and improved health outcomes. Countless stories from patients who credit the organisation with detecting their cancer early serve as powerful reminders of the life-changing difference that accessible healthcare can make.

A defining strength of PinkDrive is its collaborative approach. The organisation works closely with government departments, healthcare providers, corporate partners and civil society organisations to strengthen South Africa's public health system rather than operate independently of it. Its mobile units function as an extension of existing healthcare services, helping to reduce pressure on clinics and hospitals while expanding access to preventative care in areas where resources are limited.

This partnership-driven model has enabled PinkDrive to scale its impact while maintaining high standards of service delivery and community engagement. By combining public, private and non-profit expertise, the organisation has demonstrated how collaboration can create sustainable solutions to complex healthcare challenges.

Winning the CSI Legacy Award for Best NGO recognises PinkDrive's exceptional contribution to improving public health and reducing healthcare inequality in South Africa. It celebrates an organisation that has consistently placed compassion, dignity and accessibility at the heart of its work while proving that innovative community-based healthcare can save lives.

As South Africa continues to address the burden of cancer and unequal access to healthcare, PinkDrive stands as a powerful example of what can be achieved through purpose-driven leadership, strategic partnerships and an unwavering commitment to serving communities. Through its mobile screening services, education initiatives and advocacy efforts, the organisation is not only detecting cancer earlier—it is giving thousands of South Africans hope, improving health outcomes and creating a lasting legacy of care that will continue to save lives for generations to come.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best Rising NGO

FAMSA Johannesburg: Healing Families, Building Resilient Communities

Family Life Centre Johannesburg · Honouree Feature

Category

Best Rising NGO

Honouree

FAMSA Johannesburg

Executive Director

Jennifer Papers

Recognised

2026

All Winners

Family Life Centre Johannesburg (FAMSA) has been honoured with the CSI Legacy Award for Best Rising NGO, recognising its exceptional contribution to strengthening families, supporting vulnerable communities and expanding access to mental health and psychosocial services across Johannesburg. The award celebrates emerging organisations that are delivering innovative, measurable and sustainable social impact, and FAMSA's work stands as a powerful example of how compassionate leadership and community-based support can transform lives.

Originally established in 1949, FAMSA Johannesburg has a long history of providing counselling and family support services. In recent years, however, the organisation has experienced remarkable growth and renewed impact under the leadership of Executive Director Jennifer Papers, whose personal journey and unwavering commitment to community wellbeing have helped reposition FAMSA as one of the city's leading providers of therapeutic and family support services.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best Rising NGO is a testament to Jennifer Papers' vision of ensuring that quality therapeutic care is not a privilege reserved for a few, but a service that is accessible to families facing some of society's greatest challenges. Drawing on her own experiences as an orphan and foster child, Papers has built an organisation grounded in empathy, resilience and the belief that every family deserves the opportunity to heal and thrive.

Under her leadership, FAMSA has significantly expanded its reach into communities including Alexandra, Diepsloot, Soweto, Westbury, Lenasia South, Zakariyya Park and Parkwood, bringing much-needed psychosocial support to areas where access to mental health services is often limited. By working directly within communities, schools and families, the organisation has removed many of the barriers that prevent vulnerable individuals from receiving timely care and support.

FAMSA provides a comprehensive range of services designed to strengthen family relationships and promote emotional wellbeing. These include family and couples therapy, trauma counselling, gender-based violence (GBV) support, parenting programmes, youth development initiatives and school-based interventions. Together, these programmes address the complex social and emotional challenges that affect individuals, families and communities, while helping to break cycles of violence, conflict and intergenerational trauma.

The organisation's impact continues to grow. In the past year alone, FAMSA has reached more than 58,500 beneficiaries through counselling, crisis intervention, community outreach and preventative programmes. Each interaction represents an opportunity to restore hope, strengthen relationships and equip individuals with the skills needed to navigate adversity in healthier and more constructive ways.

A key contributor to FAMSA's recognition at the CSI Legacy Awards is its Education for Living and Anti-Bullying Programme, which is delivered in schools across Johannesburg. Recognising that many children face significant challenges both at home and within their communities, the programme creates safe spaces where learners can develop essential life skills, emotional intelligence and healthy conflict resolution techniques.

Rather than responding only after problems arise, the programme focuses on prevention by helping children build resilience, empathy, self-awareness and positive communication skills from an early age. Learners are encouraged to understand and manage their emotions, resolve conflict peacefully and develop respectful relationships with others. These skills not only improve the school environment but also influence behaviour within families and the wider community, creating positive ripple effects that extend well beyond the classroom.

What distinguishes FAMSA's approach is its understanding that healthy families are the foundation of resilient communities. By supporting individuals through trauma, strengthening family relationships and investing in the emotional wellbeing of children and young people, the organisation addresses the root causes of many social challenges rather than simply responding to their consequences.

Winning the CSI Legacy Award for Best Rising NGO recognises both the remarkable progress FAMSA has made under Jennifer Papers' leadership and the profound impact the organisation continues to have on thousands of South Africans. It is an acknowledgement of an organisation that has embraced innovation, compassion and collaboration to create meaningful, lasting change.

As the demand for accessible mental health and family support services continues to grow, FAMSA Johannesburg is demonstrating that healing individuals ultimately strengthens families, and stronger families build stronger communities. Through its dedicated team, evidence-based programmes and unwavering commitment to restoring hope, FAMSA is creating a legacy of resilience, compassion and empowerment that will continue to benefit generations to come.

About the CSI Legacy Awards

The CSI Legacy Awards is a best-practice programme that enables players in the South African CSI industry to learn from one another. In each category, programmes that have had the most positive impact on communities across the country are recognised and celebrated.

Entrants are judged by a cohort of industry experts who are unaware of the identities of the entrants — ensuring recognition is earned on merit alone.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best Green Impact Initiative

Petco: Turning Producer Responsibility into Livelihoods and a Cleaner Circular Economy

Petco · Honouree Feature

Category

Best Green Impact Initiative

Honouree

Petco

Operational Leadership

Samu Mkhize

Recognised

2026

All Winners

Petco has been honoured with the CSI Legacy Award for Best Green Impact Initiative, recognising its outstanding contribution to advancing South Africa's circular economy while creating meaningful economic opportunities for thousands of people working in the recycling sector. The award celebrates innovative environmental initiatives that deliver measurable social, economic and ecological impact, and Petco's work has demonstrated how responsible environmental stewardship can simultaneously strengthen communities, reduce waste and support sustainable livelihoods.

Established in 2004, Petco has become South Africa's leading Producer Responsibility Organisation (PRO), administering Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes on behalf of producers to ensure that packaging materials are responsibly recovered, recycled and kept within the circular economy. Through collaboration with industry, government, municipalities and communities, the organisation has helped transform the country's recycling landscape while ensuring that environmental sustainability delivers tangible benefits for people as well as the planet.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best Green Impact Initiative recognises Petco's ability to convert producer responsibility into measurable environmental and socio-economic outcomes. Under the operational leadership of Samu Mkhize, a chemical engineer and Fulbright scholar, the organisation has developed innovative programmes that address one of South Africa's most pressing environmental challenges—plastic pollution—while supporting the people who play a critical role in managing recyclable waste.

Central to Petco's award-winning approach is its commitment to strengthening the informal waste sector. Waste collectors and waste pickers are often the backbone of South Africa's recycling system, recovering significant volumes of recyclable materials despite operating under difficult conditions and with limited formal support. Recognising both their contribution and the challenges they face, Petco has invested in programmes that equip, train and empower those working on the frontline of recycling.

To date, the organisation has supported more than 4,600 waste collectors, providing practical training, equipment and access to safer, more sustainable income opportunities. By working closely with recycling cooperatives, community organisations and small businesses, Petco has helped formalise and strengthen the recycling value chain while creating opportunities for entrepreneurship and job creation.

The measurable impact of these initiatives is significant. During 2024, Petco supported 47 small, medium and micro enterprises (SMMEs), sustained 347 jobs and created 3,824 income opportunities across the recycling sector. Over the past three years, the organisation has also helped divert more than 273,000 tonnes of post-consumer packaging from landfill, ensuring that valuable materials remain in circulation rather than contributing to environmental pollution.

While these environmental outcomes are substantial, Petco's impact extends far beyond waste management. A defining feature of its work is its commitment to improving dignity, safety and inclusion for the people who make recycling possible. Waste pickers participating in Petco-supported initiatives receive personal protective equipment, improved access to safer working conditions and opportunities to participate in more formalised recycling systems that provide greater financial stability.

Women have been a particular focus of these empowerment efforts. By supporting women-led cooperatives and promoting greater participation throughout the recycling value chain, Petco has contributed to more inclusive economic development while creating opportunities for women entrepreneurs to build sustainable businesses within the green economy.

Education also plays a central role in the organisation's long-term strategy. Through awareness campaigns in schools, communities and workplaces, Petco encourages greater public participation in recycling while helping to build a culture of environmental responsibility. These initiatives not only improve recycling rates but also foster a greater understanding of the role individuals and communities can play in protecting South Africa's natural environment.

Winning the CSI Legacy Award for Best Green Impact Initiative recognises Petco's leadership in demonstrating that environmental sustainability and social development are deeply interconnected. By combining responsible producer stewardship with practical community empowerment, the organisation has created a model that benefits businesses, communities and the environment alike.

As South Africa continues its transition towards a more circular and sustainable economy, Petco stands as an inspiring example of what collaborative, purpose-driven environmental leadership can achieve. Through innovation, partnership and an unwavering commitment to both people and the planet, the organisation is reducing waste, creating livelihoods and building a greener future for generations to come. Its CSI Legacy Award is a well-deserved recognition of an initiative that is not only protecting the environment but also transforming lives through opportunity, dignity and sustainable development.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 · Best Rural Community Project

UR Global: Bringing the Digital Divide to an End, One Rural Community at a Time

Ubuntu Renaissance Global · Honouree Feature

Category

Best Rural Community Project

Honouree

UR Global

Founded By

Luleka

Recognised

2026

All Winners

UR Global has been honoured with the CSI Legacy Award for Best Rural Community Project, recognising its outstanding contribution to bridging South Africa's digital divide and creating opportunities for young people in underserved rural communities. The award celebrates initiatives that deliver meaningful, sustainable impact in rural areas, and UR Global's pioneering approach to digital inclusion is transforming lives by ensuring that geography is no longer a barrier to education, innovation or economic opportunity.

Founded by social entrepreneur Luleka, Ubuntu Renaissance Global (UR Global) was established with a clear purpose: to ensure that technology becomes a tool for inclusion rather than a source of inequality. After leaving a successful corporate career in Johannesburg, Luleka returned to her home province of the Eastern Cape, inspired by the philosophy of ubuntu and determined to give rural communities access to the same technological opportunities available in urban centres.

Her vision was shaped by personal experience. Growing up in a rural village where neighbours collectively contributed towards her school fees, she learned from an early age that community and shared responsibility have the power to change lives. Combined with her professional experience and international fellowship exposure, those formative lessons inspired the creation of an organisation committed to advancing social justice through digital inclusion and community-led development.

Receiving the CSI Legacy Award for Best Rural Community Project recognises more than a decade of dedicated work to ensure that rural learners are equipped with the digital skills needed to participate in South Africa's rapidly evolving economy. It acknowledges UR Global's belief that talent exists everywhere, but opportunity does not—and that closing this gap requires innovative solutions designed specifically for rural realities.

At the heart of UR Global's success is its flagship initiative, the Mobile Rural Technology Park (MRTP). The programme takes fully equipped mobile technology classrooms directly into rural schools and communities where access to computers, reliable electricity and internet connectivity is often limited or entirely absent. Rather than expecting learners to travel long distances to access technology, UR Global brings the technology to them.

The Mobile Rural Technology Park delivers practical training in end-user computing, coding, programming and robotics, exposing learners to skills that are increasingly essential in the Fourth Industrial Revolution. By creating engaging, hands-on learning experiences, the initiative helps build confidence while inspiring young people to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM).

What began as a pilot project serving just three schools has grown into a far-reaching programme supporting 32 schools across the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal. Over the years, thousands of learners, teachers and community members have participated in the programme, gaining practical digital skills that have opened new educational and employment opportunities.

The initiative's impact extends well beyond the classroom. Teachers receive training that enables them to integrate digital technologies into everyday learning, strengthening educational outcomes long after the mobile classrooms have moved on. Community members have used their newly acquired digital skills to improve their employability, while several learners who first encountered technology through the programme have gone on to pursue university studies in computer science and related disciplines.

A particularly significant achievement has been the programme's contribution to narrowing the gender gap in technology education. By actively encouraging girls to participate in coding, robotics and digital literacy programmes, UR Global is helping create a more inclusive technology sector while empowering young women to pursue careers in industries where they have traditionally been underrepresented.

Looking to the future, UR Global is expanding its vision beyond mobile classrooms. The organisation has already secured land in rural communities to establish permanent Rural Technology Parks that will serve as centres for digital innovation, entrepreneurship and emerging technologies. These facilities will provide ongoing access to technology, skills development and innovation hubs, ensuring that rural communities become active contributors to South Africa's digital economy rather than passive beneficiaries of technological change.

Winning the CSI Legacy Award for Best Rural Community Project is a fitting recognition of UR Global's transformative work and Luleka's inspiring leadership. Through innovation, collaboration and an unwavering belief in the potential of rural communities, the organisation is proving that where a child is born should never determine the opportunities available to them. By placing technology, education and empowerment at the centre of community development, UR Global is creating a lasting legacy of inclusion, opportunity and hope that will benefit generations to come.

Simphiwe Mtetwa Social Responsibility

We are a for-profit company with giving at our core.

Our work in social responsibility is defined by the future we are aiming for: pursuing purpose, empowering communities, and leveraging profit as a catalyst for sustainable development across Africa.

Explore Vision 2050
Impact Focus

Do good better

Our work in social responsibility is defined by the future we are aiming for; we want to see our work reflected in the lives of the people we have impacted over the years. We focus on three areas: education, housing and health/hygiene. The faces you see on our social responsibility pages speak to the world we see in 2052.

3 Areas Core Pillars
2052 Long-term Horizon
Strategic Framework

Our commitment

Revealing CSI Industry Pains

Over the years we have honed an exciting, progressive working model that informs our ten-year focus. In a nutshell: We are South Africa's innovative and growing social responsibility content creators, breaking down barriers to reveal burning social issues, or what we call CSI industry pains. We create dialogue on pertinent development issues in a bid to drive industry change.

Ten-Year Business Strategy

Our ten-year business strategy is driven by development, giving, scalability and sustainability. The aim of the strategy is not to chase profit while trying to stay ethical and law-abiding; rather, our goal is to pursue purpose through creating products, platforms, projects and campaigns that offer opportunities to other ambitious small business owners so that they, too, can serve our South African development community. We use profit as the catalyst to leverage partnerships with corporates, government and non-profit organisations.

Vision 2050

Our 30 Year Vision

Clear, quantifiable commitments to eliminate generational poverty and dignity deficits by 2050.

01

Education

One educated person in every rural household by 2050.

02

Housing

Provide 3,000 families with housing and shelter by 2050.

03

Health & Hygiene

Eradication of all pit-toilets and providing access to medical facilities to all rural communities by 2050.

Key Portfolios

Our Focus

Active initiatives where we deploy resources and establish collaborative partnerships.

Education

In education, we have two programmes – promoting access to tertiary education among high school learners and providing basic education supplies. Our goal is to ensure that every rural home in South Africa has at least one educated person, which would be sufficient to appreciably lift the standard of living of families across the country.

COMING SOON ›

Housing

Housing is the most important asset, without which scholars cannot study and entrepreneurs cannot work. We partner with leaders and use our resources to build houses for communities in need. In our housing portfolio we focus on two types of housing – Christian Churches and standard housing.

COMING SOON ›

Health & Hygiene

South African rural communities are affected by a lack of hygiene infrastructure, which affects health. Many communities continue to live without proper running toilets or safe running water. We partner with communities to build safe toilets and to provide access to health services in rural areas and townships.

COMING SOON ›
The Urgency

Why it matters

South Africa has the largest corporate social responsibility and investment spend on the African continent, and yet sits with more inequalities than any other country in the world. Our youth unemployment is a staggering 66%. This is alarming, and should matter to anyone working in the social development space in South Africa.

Social responsibility matters to us because South Africa is sitting on the brink of disaster. We have seen these dangerous conditions exploding in the form of the 2021 July looting, and in xenophobic attacks that regularly occur across the country. Anyone who earns a salary has a social responsibility, and businesses, including ours, have a responsibility to define and act on a well-considered plan to alleviate these tensions.

This is our country, and how it fares matters to us. Our progressive working model for social responsibility has a ten-year vision and a three-pronged scope: housing, education and health/hygiene.

We recently launched our dedicated social responsibility platform, the GivenGroup Foundation. This is a social investment arm funded by CSRNEWS to manage CSI funds and projects.

Through this programme, we will be advancing three causes:

Education Health Housing

We built our first Church with office space in rural Mpumalanga in 2021 with more projects to follow. The GivenGroup Foundation will be officially launched this year. We are excited about this new venture and look forward to demonstrating what can be done by a small, well-informed group on a mission.

Institutional Management

Working with bold clients to address South Africa's social challenges

The GivenGroup Foundation was established to tackle the many practical project management tasks associated with corporate social investment, and is a natural outflow from our years of CSI practice in its many diverse forms. Over the years, we have built up a team of development specialists, qualified journalists, editors and project managers who are modern, creative and forward thinking. All are steeped in the language and knowledge of CSI and able to deliver impactful projects that meet both the developmental needs of SADC countries and the demands of corporate boardrooms.

The GivenGroup Foundation is the social responsibility arm of CSRNEWS – a business dedicated to helping others reach their social responsibility goals. Our strategy is to weave Vision2050 through all of our client engagements, touching, where possible, on our own three-pronged social responsibility programme of education, housing and health/hygiene. By incorporating this vision into all facets of our work—from client counselling conversations to our analyses and recommendations—we help clients achieve their goals while addressing the fundamental needs of our society.

Through the GivenGroup, we also manage clients' projects and budgets, depending on needs. We offer a complete service that takes the hassle out of managing vast CSI programmes or parts thereof. With the GivenGroup, clients are assured of a transparent, expert and well-informed use of their funds, with full reporting given at regular phases throughout the lifespan of the project.

Speak to us about how the GivenGroup Foundation can manage your CSR budget for maximum impact, with complete transparency and accountability.

EPISODE 01

What to Do When
You Feel Overwhelmed:
A Practical Guide

What to Do When You Feel Overwhelmed
00:00 / 00:00
Episode Details Transcript
Feeling overwhelmed is something almost everyone experiences at some point. It's that sense of being pulled in multiple directions at once, where tasks, responsibilities, and expectations flood your mind and leave you unsure of where to start. In this guide, Simphiwe Mtetwa explores practical steps to regain control — especially in the workplace.

Simphiwe Mtetwa:

Feeling overwhelmed is something almost everyone experiences. A few weeks ago, I experienced it myself. My week was a cascade of tasks: emails piling up, clients calling, proposals waiting, and major events demanding attention.

Simphiwe Mtetwa:

Curious about the word itself, I discovered that "overwhelm" comes from maritime language — to be swamped by water. So what's the life jacket? For me, it was my plan. When everything was chaotic, looking at my structured plan immediately created clarity and peace.

Simphiwe Mtetwa:

Practical strategies: pause and rest, listen to your mind, prioritise using your plan, delay major decisions, and manage information intake. Feeling overwhelmed is not a weakness — it's a signal.

CSI Indaba

Article 5: Beyond 2030—Turning the CSI Indaba into a Generational Institution

Simphiwe Mtetwa August 8, 2026

Generational Accountability

The horizon provides continuity; the accountability cycle provides urgency. Each year needs a visible mandate, every cycle measurable outcomes.

The CSI Indaba was not created to become another annual date in the conference calendar. Its founding ambition is larger: to convene leaders, communities and institutions over 25 years in a sustained national effort to dismantle the structures that reproduce inequality. The 2026 classroom established the mandate. The period from 2027 to 2030 must establish the machinery. Beyond 2030, the Indaba must prove that it can sustain generational accountability.

The outcome report ends with a crucial truth: CSI cannot rewrite South Africa's social contract on its own. Corporate social-investment budgets are too small compared with the scale of the economy and the depth of exclusion. Transformation depends on the stewardship of total capital—public and private—and on the conduct of institutions that shape work, wages, ownership, procurement, investment, education, infrastructure and access to markets.

This does not make CSI irrelevant. It gives it a more strategic role. The CSI sector works close to communities, practitioners and social institutions. It sees where public systems fail, where local capability is overlooked and where promising pathways break. The Indaba can organise this knowledge, connect it to national economic debate and insist that community experience informs decisions about capital and development.

The first phase, from 2027 to 2030, should be understood as the foundation of that role. By 2030, the Indaba should have a verified baseline for the five binding constraints; a clearer map of social and development capital; a tested co-governance standard; an operating government–CSI interface; at least one independently evaluated collaborative demonstrator; and annual reporting that shows who committed to what and whether progress occurred.

These are demanding but achievable institutional milestones. They do not promise that inequality will be dismantled in four years. They ensure that the country enters the next phase with a credible system for learning, coordination and accountability.

Beyond 2030, the Indaba can deepen and expand this architecture. Successful demonstrators can be adapted across places rather than copied mechanically. Longitudinal evidence can show whether participants move into sustained education, decent work, enterprise and leadership. Capital mapping can evolve into a national intelligence platform. Community representation can mature into constituted voices with genuine mandates. Annual reports can track institutional and structural indicators across political and corporate cycles.

The 25-year horizon is essential because inequality was built over generations and will not be undone through short programmes. Yet long-term vision must never become an excuse for delayed action. Each year needs a visible mandate; every three-year cycle needs measurable outcomes; and every institution must explain its contribution within its sphere of control. The horizon provides continuity, while the accountability cycle provides urgency.

The Indaba's connection to Mandela Week gives this journey moral and practical meaning. Mandela Day has often been expressed through outside-in acts of service: institutions entering communities for a day of giving. The CSI Indaba proposes an inside-out commitment. It begins by listening to what communities know, asks institutions to examine their own power and decisions, and turns a symbolic day into a year-long developmental discipline.

This is how the Indaba can remain relevant and progressive for a generation. It can become South Africa's national classroom for testing whether the social contract is changing in practice. Are excluded people gaining voice and decision-making power? Are local institutions stronger? Are education and skills connected to real opportunity? Are markets opening? Is public capability improving? Is capital serving productive investment, employment and shared prosperity?

The next Indaba theme will eventually give language to the next stage. But the outcome is already pointing the way. The movement must be from diagnosis to compact, from charity to capability, from consultation to co-governance, from isolated projects to coordinated systems, and from annual conversation to generational accountability.

The promise of Beyond 2030 is therefore not a distant celebration. It is a standard for the choices made now. If 2026 named the inequality mandate, then 2027–2030 must build the first credible response. The years that follow must carry that response across a 25-year national journey—until inclusion is no longer an aspiration attached to a programme, but a lived reality embedded in South Africa's institutions, economy and social contract.

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Simphiwe Mtetwa is South Africa's leading Corporate Social Responsibility news, media and publishing firm. We create content on social responsibility, helping government, corporates, consultants, NPOs and NGOs to reach their target markets through appropriate, targeted development news.

CSI Indaba

Article 4: Coordination Without Confusion—Building the First 2030 Compact

Simphiwe Mtetwa August 8, 2026

The 2030 Compact

Four years to move from a shared diagnosis to a demonstrable model of coordinated action: evidence, disciplined selection and public accountability.

One of the strongest conclusions from the CSI Indaba 2026 is that disconnected projects cannot overcome structural inequality. Yet the call for coordination must be handled carefully. Not every corporate fund should be placed into one pool, and not every initiative should be forced into a national programme. The real task is to create enough alignment for collective scale while preserving innovation, local responsiveness and clear accountability.

The outcome report offers three possible approaches: pooled funding, aligned funding under a common framework, or a hybrid model. Pooled resources may be appropriate where a challenge requires scale, common infrastructure and long-term investment. Aligned funding may work better where organisations retain their own programmes but use shared outcomes, data and geographic priorities. A hybrid can combine collective investment in enabling systems with distributed delivery by capable partners.

The choice should follow the problem. It should not be driven by the desire to announce the biggest fund. Coordination without transparent governance can centralise power, increase administrative costs and move resources even further away from communities. On the other hand, refusing coordination can preserve duplication, short funding cycles and gaps between programmes that should form a single pathway.

The 2027–2030 period should become the Indaba's first compact-building window. The sector has four years to move from a shared diagnosis to a demonstrable model of coordinated action. The outcome report already identifies the foundations: a shared inequality baseline, capital and portfolio mapping, a community co-governance standard, a government–CSI delivery compact, common capability measures, shared services, quarterly classrooms and an independently evaluated demonstrator.

The first step is evidence. South Africa still lacks a verified map of all major social-investment and development capital flows. Without it, claims about scale and allocation remain partial. A capital map should show what is funded, where, for whom, through which intermediaries, and against which binding constraint. Combined with a place-based baseline, it can reveal duplication, neglect and opportunities for alignment.

The second step is disciplined selection. The Indaba should choose one collaborative demonstrator at meaningful scale—place-based or thematic—and establish a baseline before implementation. The initiative should have independent governance, legitimate community decision-making, named owners, audited reporting and a three-year outcome horizon. Its purpose would not be to claim that one project has solved inequality. It would test whether the principles articulated in 2026 can operate together in practice.

The third step is public accountability. Every agreed action needs an owner, deadline, status and next review date. Quarterly classrooms should review evidence, explain delays and publish decisions. An annual outcome report should capture movement, not merely restate speeches. At the end of the first cycle, an independent evaluation should assess change at system, institutional and participant levels.

This compact must also connect CSI and BBBEE rather than treating them as unrelated sectors. The five binding constraints intertwine with ownership, procurement, skills, employment, enterprise and institutional power. Corporate responsibility cannot be divided neatly between a philanthropic portfolio and the rest of the business. Social and ethics committees should consider how core operations and CSI jointly affect inequality.

If this architecture is built between 2027 and 2030, "Beyond 2030" gains substance. It becomes the point at which the Indaba can scale what has been tested, correct what has failed and enter its next phase with evidence rather than aspiration. The 25-year journey then has a working accountability system: shared baselines, visible commitments, legitimate participation and annual public learning.

But coordination is still a means, not the final purpose. The deepest question remains: what kind of South Africa is this compact trying to create, and how should the totality of national capital serve that vision? The final article takes the series beyond a CSI strategy and towards a renewed social contract for 2030 and the generations that follow.

Article 3: Fund What Must Endure—From Projects to Institutions and Capability

Simphiwe Mtetwa August 8, 2026

Impact Infrastructure

Shared services, practitioner networks and institutional diagnostics are not secondary expenses. They are the building blocks of lasting change.

South Africa is filled with the remains of well-intentioned development: facilities that cannot be maintained, gardens without functioning water systems, digital equipment without connectivity, and programmes that disappear when a funding cycle closes. These failures are not always caused by poor intentions. They often begin with a model that rewards visible activity but underinvests in the people and institutions required to sustain it.

The CSI Indaba 2026 outcome report proposes a more demanding test: judge CSI by what it builds, what continues and who becomes more independent—not only by money announced, beneficiaries counted or ceremonies held.

This does not mean immediate relief should disappear. People experiencing hunger, violence, unemployment or educational exclusion cannot wait for a long-term system to be redesigned. The report keeps this tension visible: social-investment portfolios must respond to urgent need while deliberately connecting relief to structural action. The question is whether today's intervention also strengthens tomorrow's capacity.

Capability must therefore become a recognised investment outcome. It includes the ability of a community organisation to govern itself, retain skilled people, manage finance, use data, comply proportionately and attract diverse funding. It includes the ability of a municipality or public department to prepare projects, coordinate delivery and maintain public assets. It includes the agency of participants to navigate education, employment, enterprise and civic institutions without permanent programme dependency.

This changes how success is measured. Training attendance is not the same as institutional capability. A new facility is not an outcome if it is unusable five years later. A funded organisation is not independent if it collapses as soon as one donor exits. A learner programme is incomplete if it has no connection to further study, work experience, employment or enterprise.

For 2027–2030, the Indaba should champion lifecycle and ecosystem planning. Before a physical asset is funded, partners should understand who will own it, operate it, maintain it and finance its future. Before a youth initiative begins, the programme should map the pathway from recruitment to recognised skills and real opportunity. Before a small organisation is declared "not ready", funders should identify whether targeted capacity support could make it ready.

The report proposes practical building blocks: shared finance and compliance services; practitioner networks; municipal and institutional diagnostics; support for registration pathways; and measures of agency, ownership, institutional strength and post-funding continuation. These are not secondary administrative expenses. They are impact infrastructure.

This is also where the government–CSI relationship must mature. CSI cannot substitute for the state by creating parallel delivery systems indefinitely. Nor should public institutions reject useful expertise simply because it comes from outside government. The goal is an accountable partnership that strengthens the developmental state while preserving clear public responsibility. Business, academia and civil society can contribute technical knowledge and resources, but they must not erase the state's mandate or allow responsibility to dissolve into collaboration rhetoric.

By 2030, the Indaba should be able to point to institutions that are measurably stronger because the sector changed what it funded. That evidence might include community organisations with diversified income and retained leadership; public facilities still operating; municipalities with improved service outcomes; social enterprises moving from capacity support to finance; or young people progressing through complete pathways rather than disconnected activities.

Over a 25-year horizon, institutional memory matters as much as programme innovation. Each annual Indaba should add to a living account of what endured, what failed and why. That record can protect the sector from repeatedly funding new versions of old mistakes.

However, stronger institutions working separately will still struggle against interconnected inequality. Capability creates the foundation, but scale requires coordination. The fourth article examines how the sector can align resources without creating a single fund, a new bureaucracy or a place where shared responsibility becomes nobody's responsibility.

Article 2: Communities Cannot Remain Beneficiaries of Other People's Decisions

Simphiwe Mtetwa August 8, 2026

Co-Authors of Development

Communities must participate from diagnosis through design, governance and evaluation — a shift in authority, not merely respectful engagement.

The CSI Indaba 2026 produced a decisive challenge to one of the social-investment sector's oldest habits: communities are too often invited into the room after priorities, budgets and measures of success have already been determined. They may be consulted, counted or photographed, but they seldom hold meaningful decision-making power.

The outcome report calls for a fundamental correction. Communities must participate from diagnosis through design, implementation, governance and evaluation. This is more than respectful engagement. It is a shift in authority—from treating people as recipients of institutional generosity to recognising them as co-authors of development.

This shift matters because lived experience contains intelligence that formal systems frequently miss. Community leaders know which facilities are failing, which routes are unaffordable, which young people have disappeared from the education pipeline, and why a technically sound programme may not survive local realities. Asset-based community design begins with what people already do, value and organise, rather than beginning with an external institution's predetermined solution.

The report also warns that "community voice" cannot become another slogan. Representation must be legitimate. Who has a mandate to speak? How are representatives selected? What decision rights do they hold? How does information return to the constituency? Without answers, the language of participation can conceal the same power arrangements it claims to change.

The 2027–2030 planning period must therefore establish a community co-governance standard for the Indaba and its partners. At minimum, this should define representation, voting rights, feedback loops and the proportion of priorities originating from communities themselves. Grassroots organisations should participate in investment committees and programme governance, not merely implementation. Public reporting should show how community input changed a decision, a budget or a delivery model.

This approach requires funders to examine their own systems. Governance and compliance remain necessary because public-purpose capital must be protected. However, compliance should be proportionate to the funding and risk involved, and institutional readiness should be built rather than used only as an exclusion threshold. If capable local organisations are rejected because they lack finance, monitoring or digital systems, the appropriate response may be to invest in those systems—not to redirect the work automatically to a large intermediary.

Flexible institutional support is especially important. Many local founders carry deep knowledge and trust but cannot pay themselves, retain staff or manage growing administrative demands. They eventually leave the community organisation to earn a living inside a larger NGO, taking irreplaceable knowledge with them. If CSI only funds activities and never the institution delivering them, it weakens the very infrastructure on which sustainable change depends.

Between 2027 and 2030, the Indaba can demonstrate a different model. It can create shared services for finance, compliance, human resources, monitoring and proposal development. It can make support accessible through low-bandwidth channels. It can track how much funding reaches locally led and rural organisations after intermediary costs. Most importantly, it can test whether communities become more capable, organised and powerful—not only whether more services are delivered to them.

This is how the 25-year vision begins to take practical form. Dismantling inequality is not simply about redistributing resources within existing relationships. It is about changing who defines the problem, who controls capital and who judges success. By 2030, the Indaba should be able to show that community co-governance has moved from aspiration to standard practice among participating partners.

Yet transferring voice without strengthening institutions can leave communities holding responsibility without the means to act. The next article therefore turns to the infrastructure of transformation: the organisations, public systems and local capabilities that must remain standing long after individual grants have ended.

Article 1: The Indaba Has Diagnosed the Crisis—Now the Work Must Begin

Simphiwe Mtetwa August 8, 2026

The Indaba's Diagnosis

The CSI Indaba 2026 outcome report establishes a shared diagnosis of inequality and a 25-year mandate to dismantle it.

South Africa does not need another gathering where inequality is described with eloquence and then left unchanged. This conviction gave birth to the CSI Indaba 2026, convened as South Africa's Biggest CSI Classroom. For two days, leaders from business, government, civil society, academia and communities examined why three decades of corporate social investment have not shifted inequality at the scale the country demands.

The outcome report is clear: the problem is not a shortage of goodwill. South Africa has thousands of social programmes, committed practitioners and organisations doing difficult work. Yet their efforts operate within systems that continue to reproduce unequal opportunity. Spatial exclusion determines how far people must travel to reach work, education and services. Skills mismatches leave qualifications disconnected from economic demand. Market concentration limits ownership and entry. Weak governance damages delivery and trust. A dysfunctional labour market keeps millions outside meaningful economic participation.

These are not separate social problems. They reinforce one another. A learner in a rural community may experience weak early childhood development, poor digital access, limited career guidance and unaffordable transport long before reaching the labour market. A small local organisation may understand that learner's circumstances but remain excluded from funding because it lacks the administrative systems demanded by large institutions. A young entrepreneur may complete a programme yet find no route to finance, procurement or markets. Activity has taken place, but the architecture of exclusion remains.

This is why the first outcome of the Indaba matters: CSI portfolios must be linked to a shared diagnosis of inequality rather than broad themes alone. It is no longer sufficient to say an initiative supports "education", "youth" or "enterprise". We must ask which binding constraint it is changing, in which place, for whom, and what will be different when the funding ends.

The report also places an important boundary around CSI. Corporate social investment matters, but CSI budgets cannot carry the full burden of national transformation. Inequality is shaped by public policy, municipal capability, core business investment, employment practices, wages, procurement, ownership and access to markets. A company cannot use a small philanthropic budget to compensate for economic decisions that deepen exclusion elsewhere. Equally, the private sector cannot treat the state as the only source of failure. Rewriting the social contract requires each institution to accept responsibility within its sphere of power.

For the CSI Indaba, 2026 was therefore not the year of final answers. It was Year One of a 25-year journey: the year in which the classroom named the system, surfaced its contradictions and established a mandate to dismantle inequality. The outcome report should not be treated as a commemorative publication. It is a baseline against which the sector must judge what happens next.

The first test comes in 2027. The Indaba must move from diagnosis to a disciplined accountability cycle. It must confirm the evidence, clarify the language of impact, establish legitimate community representation, appoint owners to agreed actions and publish deadlines. It must also choose where to concentrate collective effort. If every problem is declared a priority, fragmentation will simply return under a new banner.

The opportunity is profound. The Indaba can become the place where social-investment actors stop presenting isolated success stories and begin building a shared national account of change. It can connect local experience to national strategy, and corporate resources to public and community capability. It can make the invisible visible: who decides, who benefits, which institutions become stronger and whether opportunity actually expands.

But diagnosis alone does not transfer power. If the 2026 classroom has established what is wrong, the next question is more difficult: who will have the authority to decide what must be built? That question takes us to the second article in this series—the movement from beneficiaries to co-authors of South Africa's social contract.
