CSI Manager of The Year – Vovo Ngcwabe – Cultivating Seeds of Social Change Through Mbewu

Simphiwe Mtetwa

The Mbewu Fund

A pioneering initiative designed to activate social enterprises that continue to flourish in local communities.

Listen

Audio version of this article

Recognised as the CSI Manager of the Year through the CSI Legacy Awards, Vovo has become a leading figure in Corporate Social Investment in South Africa. Her innovative leadership and passion for sustainable development have played a central role in the success of the Mbewu Social Fund, a pioneering initiative she helped design while serving at Barloworld. Today, as Non-Executive Director of the fund, her influence continues to shape the way corporates engage with social change.

"I am currently the Non-Executive Director to the Mbewu Social Fund, having exited full-time employment with Barloworld in September 2022," Vovo explains. "I'm a social entrepreneur at heart, and I was privileged to design the fund which launched in 2019. Since then, it has activated a number of social enterprises that continue to flourish in local communities, addressing challenges through a business lens and adapting innovative solutions to create social impact."

The word Mbewu, meaning "seed" in isiZulu, encapsulates the fund's core philosophy — to plant the beginnings of change that multiply over time. "We deliberately chose the name to reflect the idea of seeding a better future. Think about how many seeds are in an apple, and in turn, how many apples are in a seed. Our intention was to plant as many of these seeds as possible — creating initiatives that not only feed communities but help them reimagine their own futures by leveraging their internal strengths and community assets."

Mbewu was born out of a realisation that many promising social entrepreneurs were falling through the cracks. "We kept receiving requests from brilliant young people whose ventures didn't quite meet traditional funding criteria," she recalls. "We believed there had to be a model that provided resources — not just funding, but governance, registration and legal support — that mirrored corporate compliance. Many social impact organisations, especially in under-resourced communities, struggle to meet these standards. Mbewu was designed to fill that gap."

The programme's development was rooted in deep collaboration. "We undertook extensive research and consulted both within Barloworld and externally. Getting internal buy-in was crucial — it elevated the programme to a strategic level and ensured the financial support it needed. We also ensured that it aligned with the company's broader sustainability agenda and transformation targets, particularly under the Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment framework. This gave us a solid foundation to develop community-focused solutions that also served the company's long-term interests."

A key strength of Mbewu has been its ability to stay aligned with Barloworld's business values while delivering tangible impact for beneficiaries. "We anchored all our efforts on the corporate sustainability pillars, especially the social pillar. We carefully selected beneficiaries whose work aligned with our goals; while also ensuring they served the needs of their own communities. When communities prosper, the businesses supporting them also benefit — it's a mutually reinforcing ecosystem."

While many CSI programmes struggle with long-term sustainability, Mbewu has endured by staying intentional. "We built the programme to align with the company's long-term goals and placed sustainability at its core. Our focus areas were informed by this vision, and we made a point of truly understanding the communities we served."

Asked about the broader role of corporates in tackling South Africa's most pressing social challenges — from education inequality to youth unemployment — Vovo is unequivocal: "CSI programmes have historically contributed to access to quality education, but inequality is complex and requires multiple interventions. Supporting local SMMEs is one powerful way to create jobs and provide vocational training for young people. This gives them the exposure and experience they need."

Looking to the future, she sees the intersection between sustainable development and food security as a key opportunity for CSI. "We need to support green economies, integrate digital technologies into impact reporting, and redirect resources where they're needed most. With climate-related disasters on the rise — from cyclones in the Indian Ocean to droughts in the western regions — future CSI initiatives will have to be agile and technologically equipped to respond effectively."

Winning the CSI Legacy Award in 2024, she says, has been a powerful validation of her team's work. "It meant a great deal to us — it confirmed that we were on the right path by listening to the needs of our beneficiaries. For me personally, it was thrilling to see the outside world recognise that impactful, innovative programmes can be developed within corporate spaces. These are world-class initiatives, grounded in solid research."

For those just starting out in the CSI space, her advice is clear: "Build partnerships with like-minded organisations and academic institutions. This will give you a strong theoretical grounding which you can then test within a corporate environment. Internally, find an executive sponsor who will advocate for your ideas at leadership level — and seek out a mentor to guide you along the way."

Vovo's journey is proof that social investment, when done with vision and integrity, can plant the seeds for transformational change — not only for communities, but for the future of Corporate South Africa itself.

Why Inequality Persists: Slaves Made a Deal with Their Masters and The Children of The Slaves Continue to Uphold the Masters' Deal

Simphiwe Mtetwa

About This Article

A deep exploration of South Africa's historical context and the structural foundations of inequality that persist today.

Listen

Audio version of this article

There is a detail from South Africa's corporate history that deserves far greater attention than it receives — and it belongs, fittingly, at the beginning of this story. In the mid-1980s, as apartheid entered its final phase and pressure mounted both domestically and internationally, Anglo-American, the most powerful mining conglomerate in the country at the time, did not simply wait for history to unfold. It prepared for it. Under the leadership of its chairman Gavin Relly, and driven by executive Clem Sunter, the company developed a series of scenario-planning models that would later become widely known as the "High Road" and the "Low Road". The Low Road envisioned a future in which minority rule clung to power, plunging the country into conflict and economic collapse. The High Road imagined a negotiated transition to democracy and South Africa's reintegration into the global economy.

These were not abstract exercises. Sunter presented these scenarios to the cabinet of F. W. de Klerk and engaged, shortly before his release, with Nelson Mandela. By the early 1990s, the Montfleur Scenario Exercise had expanded this work, bringing together political leaders, business figures, trade unionists and intellectuals to map the country's possible futures. Business, in other words, had done its arithmetic long before the negotiations began. It had examined the full range of outcomes, calculated what would need to be conceded to preserve the system, and quietly determined that what it was willing to offer would be only a fraction of what it possessed. That is the context—deliberate, calculated, and historically documented—in which one must understand a striking insight from Steven Friedman.

Slaves made a deal with their masters!

It is an image that is difficult to shake: think about it, slaves seated at a table, negotiating with their masters. The force of that idea became clearer to me through an entirely ordinary, domestic experience. Recently, I had to carry out some maintenance on my house. There were cracked tiles, peeling paint, and a roof beginning to yield to the Johannesburg rains. I sat down and worked through the costs — tiles, waterproofing, sealant, labour — and arrived at a figure of roughly R10,000. Enough to see the house safely through winter. But there was something I did not say aloud at the time. I could afford R10,000 precisely because I had considerably more than R10,000. My willingness to spend that amount rested on a quiet certainty: that doing so would not destabilise me. The apparent generosity of the gesture — if it can even be called that — was entirely relative to what remained unseen.

That small moment stayed with me long after the last tile had been laid. This moment serves, in its own quiet way, as a precise metaphor for how inequality in South Africa was constructed—and why, thirty years into democracy, it persists. As liberation became inevitable, those who controlled economic power did not simply yield. They prepared. They calculated, with care, how much they were willing to place on the table—and they ensured that what they offered would not threaten what they intended to keep. Those who came to sit across from them arrived from an entirely different position. They had been worn down by decades of deliberate exclusion. Many were encountering, for the first time, the full material weight of what had long been denied to them. The table was not merely inviting; it was overwhelming. So, understandably, the instinct was to sit at the table and partake in what had always been withheld.

This is not a moral judgement on those who negotiated the transition. It is an observation about power, context and human psychology. When a door has been closed to you for a lifetime, your first impulse when it opens is not to question the architecture of the room. It is to step inside. Yet the room — and the table within it — had already been designed. This is the foundation of Friedman's central argument: that South Africa is divided not simply by race or class, but by a more enduring distinction between insiders and outsiders. Insiders are those connected to the formal economy – earning, investing, and accumulating. Outsiders remain structurally excluded from these systems.

Under apartheid, this divide was explicitly racial. Today, it is formally economic, though still deeply shaped by the racial architecture of the past. What is striking is not only that the divide persists but also that the original settlement produced a particular kind of insider class — one that inherited access to the economy but not necessarily the freedom to reimagine it. The children of that transition now manage what was conceded, often guided by a psychological inheritance shaped by scarcity, exclusion and the urgency to secure what had previously been denied.

Human development research consistently shows that early childhood — those formative years between birth and roughly seven — leaves a lasting imprint. Values, anxieties and assumptions about the world are absorbed long before they are consciously examined. A child raised in an environment defined by exclusion and precarity does not simply shed those conditions when circumstances improve. The imprint remains, often subtly shaping decisions about risk, wealth and belonging. This is part of the reason inequality proves so stubborn. It is not sustained by policies alone but by deeply embedded patterns of thought and behaviour.

It is reinforced, too, by the values that dominate public life. Worth continues to be measured in terms of wealth, consumption and visible success. The priorities of society reflect the interests of insiders. When water shortages affect suburban households, the response is swift and urgent. When similar or worse conditions persist in townships and rural areas, they often receive less attention. Even the proposed solutions often reproduce the problem. There is near-universal agreement that formal employment is the primary path out of inequality. Yet formal employment is shrinking globally, including in South Africa. Meanwhile, millions sustain themselves through informal economic activity that is dynamic, adaptive and resilient.

Too often, corporate social investment programmes are designed to "formalise" these livelihoods, rather than to support and strengthen them on their own terms. Similarly, social grants are frequently dismissed as fostering dependency. Yet evidence consistently shows that they stimulate local economies and enable recipients to pursue additional sources of income. Properly understood, they are not a burden but a foundation. What Friedman ultimately calls for is not incremental reform, but a shift in imagination — a willingness to confront the structural limits embedded in the original settlement.

Those who came to the negotiating table with power understood something fundamental: you can only give away what you are prepared to lose. What was offered was carefully calibrated. It was enough to secure transition, but not enough to fundamentally redistribute power. Thirty years later, South Africa remains shaped by that calculation. The challenge now is not simply to do more within the existing framework but to question the framework itself. The corporate social investment sector, along with anyone committed to dismantling inequality, faces the task of not only increasing outputs but also expanding participation, reducing exclusion, and deliberately reshaping the underlying architecture of the economy. Because, in the end, the work required is not cosmetic. The renovation goes far deeper than the tiles.

The Future of Corporate Social Investment in South Africa: Navigating the Next 30 Years

Simphiwe Mtetwa

The Next 30 Years

Exploring emerging trends and strategies that will define success in the decades to come.

As South Africa looks ahead, the landscape of Corporate Social Investment (CSI) is poised for further evolution. With the challenges and opportunities of the past 30 years as a backdrop, CSI practitioners must now anticipate and navigate a rapidly changing socio-economic environment. This article explores the future of CSI in South Africa, offering insights on emerging trends and the strategies that will define success in the decades to come.

The next 30 years present both challenges and opportunities for CSI practitioners in South Africa. By embracing technological advancements, prioritising sustainability, promoting social equity, and investing in health and wellbeing, CSI can continue to drive meaningful social change.

Through collaborative approaches, data-driven decision making, agility, and community engagement, CSI practitioners can navigate the future effectively. The NGOs that thrive will be those that align with the emerging trends and adopt innovative approaches to social development.

  • Tech-Driven NGOs: Organisations that leverage technology to address social issues will be well-positioned for success. Examples include NGOs that use digital platforms for education, telemedicine for healthcare delivery, and data analytics for impact assessment.
  • Environmental NGOs: With sustainability becoming a central focus, NGOs dedicated to environmental conservation, renewable energy, and climate resilience will play a critical role. These organisations will work on projects ranging from reforestation and wildlife conservation to sustainable farming practices and clean energy initiatives.
  • Social Enterprise NGOs: NGOs that operate as social enterprises, generating income while addressing social challenges, will thrive. These organisations can create sustainable revenue streams through innovative business models, reducing dependency on traditional funding sources.
  • Inclusive Development NGOs: NGOs that focus on promoting social equity and inclusion will remain crucial. These organisations will work on initiatives that empower marginalised groups, promote gender equality, and support economic inclusion through skills training and entrepreneurship programmes.

Conclusion

The next 30 years present both challenges and opportunities for CSI practitioners in South Africa. By embracing technological advancements, prioritising sustainability, promoting social equity, and investing in health and wellbeing, CSI can continue to drive meaningful social change.

Through collaborative approaches, data-driven decision making, agility, and community engagement, CSI practitioners can navigate the future effectively. The NGOs that thrive will be those that align with these trends and adopt innovative, inclusive, and sustainable approaches to social development.

Shaping the Future of After School Care in South Africa: The Role of Corporate Social Investment in 2050

Simphiwe Mtetwa

The Year 2050

Envisioning the landscape of after school care and the crucial role CSI will play in shaping this future.

In envisioning the landscape of after school care in South Africa in 2050, one cannot overlook the crucial role that Corporate Social Investment (CSI) will play in shaping and preparing for this future. The evolving needs of children, families, and communities will require innovative and sustainable solutions, making it imperative for businesses to invest in the well-being and development of the next generation.

As we fast forward to 2050, after school care in South Africa will have undergone significant transformations to meet the changing needs of children and families. The traditional model of after school programmes will have expanded to encompass a holistic approach that not only provides academic support but also focuses on emotional intelligence, life skills, and extracurricular activities.

These programmes will be designed to cater to the unique strengths and challenges of each child, fostering a sense of belonging, resilience, and self-confidence. Furthermore, technology will play a pivotal role in shaping after school care in 2050. Virtual learning platforms, AI-driven tutoring programmes, and remote mentoring opportunities will enable children to access quality education and support from anywhere, bridging the gap between urban and rural areas.

In addition, schools and community centres will serve as hubs for innovation and creativity, offering maker spaces, coding clubs, and entrepreneurship workshops to nurture the next generation of leaders and changemakers.

Corporate Social Investment will be a driving force in shaping the future of after school care in South Africa. Companies will recognize the importance of investing in education, youth development, and community empowerment as a strategic imperative to drive long-term social impact and sustainable growth.

By partnering with schools, NGOs, and government agencies, businesses can leverage their resources, expertise, and networks to create innovative after school programs that address the diverse needs of children and families. CSI initiatives in 2050 will go beyond financial donations to promote employee volunteering, skills development, and mentorship programs. Employees will be encouraged to actively engage with local communities, sharing their knowledge and experience to support children in their educational journey.

Furthermore, businesses will collaborate with academia, research institutions, and civil society organizations to co-create evidence-based interventions that deliver measurable outcomes and drive systemic change in after school care.

In conclusion, the future of after school care in South Africa in 2050 holds great promise for nurturing the potential of every child and building resilient communities. Corporate Social Investment will be instrumental in shaping this future by fostering collaboration, innovation, and impact-driven initiatives that empower children to succeed in a rapidly changing world. By investing in after school care today, businesses can lay the foundation for a brighter tomorrow where every child has the opportunity to thrive and reach their full potential.

Why Inequality Persists: Slaves Made a Deal with Their Masters and The Children of The Slaves Continue to uphold the Masters' Deal

Simphiwe Mtetwa

The Masters' Deal

A detail from South Africa's corporate history that deserves far greater attention than it receives.

There is a detail from South Africa's corporate history that deserves far greater attention than it receives — and it belongs, fittingly, at the beginning of this story. In the mid-1980s, as apartheid entered its final phase and pressure mounted both domestically and internationally, Anglo-American, the most powerful mining conglomerate in the country at the time, did not simply wait for history to unfold. It prepared for it. Under the leadership of its chairman Gavin Relly, and driven by executive Clem Sunter, the company developed a series of scenario-planning models that would later become widely known as the "High Road" and the "Low Road".

The Low Road envisioned a future in which minority rule clung to power, plunging the country into conflict and economic collapse. The High Road imagined a negotiated transition to democracy and South Africa's reintegration into the global economy.

These were not abstract exercises. Sunter presented these scenarios to the cabinet of F. W. de Klerk and engaged, shortly before his release, with Nelson Mandela. By the early 1990s, the Montfleur Scenario Exercise had expanded this work, bringing together political leaders, business figures, trade unionists and intellectuals to map the country's possible futures. Business, in other words, had done its arithmetic long before the negotiations began.

It had examined the full range of outcomes, calculated what would need to be conceded to preserve the system, and quietly determined that what it was willing to offer would be only a fraction of what it possessed. That is the context—deliberate, calculated, and historically documented—in which one must understand a striking insight from Steven Friedman.

Slaves made a deal with their masters!

It is an image that is difficult to shake: think about it, slaves seated at a table, negotiating with their masters. The force of that idea became clearer to me through an entirely ordinary, domestic experience. Recently, I had to carry out some maintenance on my house. There were cracked tiles, peeling paint, and a roof beginning to yield to the Johannesburg rains. I sat down and worked through the costs — tiles, waterproofing, sealant, labour — and arrived at a figure of roughly R10,000. Enough to see the house safely through winter.

But there was something I did not say aloud at the time. I could afford R10,000 precisely because I had considerably more than R10,000. My willingness to spend that amount rested on a quiet certainty: that doing so would not destabilise me. The apparent generosity of the gesture — if it can even be called that — was entirely relative to what remained unseen.

That small moment stayed with me long after the last tile had been laid. This moment serves, in its own quiet way, as a precise metaphor for how inequality in South Africa was constructed—and why, thirty years into democracy, it persists. As liberation became inevitable, those who controlled economic power did not simply yield. They prepared. They calculated, with care, how much they were willing to place on the table—and they ensured that what they offered would not threaten what they intended to keep.

Those who came to sit across from them arrived from an entirely different position. They had been worn down by decades of deliberate exclusion. Many were encountering, for the first time, the full material weight of what had long been denied to them. The table was not merely inviting; it was overwhelming. So, understandably, the instinct was to sit at the table and partake in what had always been withheld.

Simphiwe Mtetwa

A 25-Year Vision in Motion
Editor's View, South Africa

A 25-Year Vision in Motion

Simphiwe Mtetwa

The CSI Indaba

A 25-year vision to transform the CSI landscape through meaningful dialogue and strategic partnerships.

What an extraordinary month this has been. As you read this—perhaps early in the morning—my team and I are convening a private Intellectual Foundation session with Professor Steven Friedman of the University of Johannesburg. This closed session brings together confirmed and conditional speakers for the CSI Indaba, and marks a critical step in shaping the depth, direction and intellectual integrity of what we are building.

From the outset, we have been intentional about what the CSI Indaba must be. Not simply another convening, but a platform that delivers clear value, sharp thinking, and meaningful contribution to the sector. The Intellectual Foundation sessions are a key part of that intent—ensuring that what is presented on stage aligns with what our delegates truly need from this space.

This does not exist in isolation. South Africa is home to many exceptional platforms advancing the CSI agenda, and we acknowledge the role they continue to play in driving growth and transformation across the sector. We have learned from them, and we respect the ground they have laid. At the same time, we are building something distinct.

I would like to extend my sincere thanks to every individual who submitted a speaker proposal earlier this year. Each 600-word submission represented not only an idea, but a commitment to shaping the future of CSI. We read every single one—personally, I read nearly all of them in full. That process was important to us. It was about recognising your voice, your thinking, and your contribution to this industry.

To those selected as speakers—congratulations. To those in the conditional category—congratulations. And to those not selected this year, this is not a reflection of your work, but rather a reflection of a very deliberate and focused first-year agenda.

Because the CSI Indaba is not a once-off event. It is a 25-year vision. What you are beginning to see now—monthly webinars, ongoing podcast conversations, curated engagements—is the start of a continuum. A build-up that is responsive to the sector, aligned to your needs, and designed to deepen the quality of discourse long before we gather in person.

We are also seeing new audiences emerge, alongside a broader and more diverse set of partners joining this journey. That, in itself, is a powerful signal of what is possible. Tickets are now at full price, and I encourage you to secure your place. Those who join us early—particularly in April—will gain access to our full webinar series at no additional cost. These sessions are not supplementary; they are foundational to the Indaba experience.

In the coming months, we will be joined by voices such as clinical psychologist Nomfundo Mogapi, among others, as we continue to build towards a programme that is both rigorous and relevant. As you consider your participation, I encourage you to be deliberate. Be clear about what you seek to gain, and equally clear about what you intend to contribute.

Because ultimately, our collective responsibility is simple: to drive impact, enable progress, and serve our communities with integrity—while ensuring that the work we do is recognised, valued, and properly compensated. This is the work. And this is just the beginning.

Unemployment Is Costing South Africans Half A Trillion Rand Annually In Lost GDP.

Simphiwe Mtetwa
March 23, 2026 • 4 min read

South Africa's unemployment crisis is no longer simply a labour market problem. It is the single largest structural drag on the country's economic output, social cohesion, and long-term sustainability. With over 7.8 million people officially unemployed — a rate of 31.4% — and a further 12.4 million excluded when discouraged workers are included, the cost to the economy is not just human. It is profoundly financial.

Now let us get to what got you here for — the figure in this article's headline is theoretical. No government publication or academic study has stamped it with definitive authority — and that absence is itself telling. But the observation is defensible, and the methodology is straightforward. These 7.8 million people are not incapable of contributing to the economy. They have been structurally excluded from it. If even a significant portion were to enter the formal labour market at South Africa's current national minimum wage of R4,606 per month — the legal floor for full-time work as of March 2025 — their combined wage contribution alone would approach R430 billion annually.

Add the taxes they would pay, the consumer spending they would generate, and the approximately R33 billion the state currently spends on social relief grants that many of them receive, and the total economic value of their participation moves comfortably toward half a trillion rand every year.

This is not a precise calculation. It is a grounded, conservative observation — and it matters, because it reframes unemployment from a social challenge into an economic one. South Africa is not simply failing millions of people. It is leaving a vast portion of its potential GDP on the table every single year.

This is precisely the kind of conversation that the CSI Indaba exists to have — and to move beyond having. The Indaba is not a gathering where uncomfortable numbers are aired and then set aside. It is the space where South Africa's corporate, civil society, and government leaders are challenged to sit with those numbers, interrogate them honestly, and leave with a shared commitment to act on them.

Unemployment. Inequality. The structural limits of what CSI, as currently designed, can achieve. These are not peripheral topics at the Indaba. They are the centre of it.

Against this backdrop, Corporate Social Investment operates at a vastly different scale. Total CSI expenditure in South Africa sits at approximately R13 billion annually. The point of highlighting this figure is because I believe we need to reframe what we ask of it.

For decades, CSI has been structured to respond to the symptoms of inequality — funding education, health, food security, and community programmes. These interventions are necessary. Many are life-changing. But they do not fundamentally alter the structural dynamics that keep millions of people excluded from economic participation. They were never designed to.

Unemployment at this scale is a systemic market failure — rooted in the disconnect between education and industry, in spatial inequality, in barriers to entry for small businesses, and in an economy that has not grown inclusively enough to absorb its labour force. South Africa needs real GDP growth of at least 3.5% annually to make a meaningful dent in unemployment, yet in 2024, real GDP grew by just 0.6%. Fragmented interventions, however well-intentioned, cannot bridge that gap. What is required is coordinated, long-term, system-level thinking.

This is where the opportunity for CSI lies — not as a primary funder of solutions, but as a catalyst for systemic change.

As the CSI Indaba begins its 25-year journey, one target emerges as both ambitious and necessary: contributing towards reducing the economic cost of unemployment by at least 10% by 2050. Even on our conservative estimate, a 10% reduction means close to R50 billion restored to the economy annually — not cumulatively, but every single year. The multiplier effects of increased consumption, higher tax revenues, and reduced social dependency would amplify this further still.

Four shifts are required to get there. First, CSI must de-risk innovation in job creation — backing early-stage models that connect skills directly to employment, and absorbing the risk that the market will not. Second, it must build pathways rather than projects: integrated pipelines from education through to enterprise creation and job placement, funding the connective tissue that isolated interventions consistently miss. Third, it must invest more deliberately in the informal and township economy — one of the most under-leveraged job creation engines in the country. And fourth, it must act as a convener, bringing corporates, government, civil society, and capital markets into genuine alignment around shared goals and measurable outcomes.

That last point matters more than it might appear. The conversation can no longer be defined only by how much is being spent. It must be defined by how effectively that spend contributes to reducing structural unemployment. Expenditure without accountability is not investment — it is optics.

South Africa does not lack goodwill. It does not lack capital. What it requires is alignment at scale, and a willingness to treat social investment as an economic lever — not just a moral obligation.
The cost of doing nothing is already being counted. The question is whether we are willing to count it honestly — and act accordingly.

Simphiwe Mtetwa

The Phantom Enforcers of Inequality: Rethinking South Africa's Social Contract

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

5 minutes

Category

Social Inequality

There is a Christian Holy Bible scripture that has stayed with me for many years — one that continues to humble me every time I return to it. It speaks to the idea that if we think we know, we do not yet know as we ought to know. Over time, I have come to understand that this is not a dismissal of knowledge, but rather a warning against certainty.

In preparing for the inaugural conference, I have experienced that humility more deeply than ever before. Over the past few months, I have spent countless hours reading inequality reports, engaging with researchers, and sitting in rigorous late-night discussions with our speaker and programme committee — respected professors, doctors, practitioners, and leaders who have challenged every assumption we thought we understood.

In many ways, the process has been uncomfortable. There were moments where I realised that some of our earlier thinking was too broad, too simplistic, or too ambitious without fully appreciating the complexity of the challenges before us. For that, I believe an apology is necessary.

An apology for the moments where our language may have suggested that inequality is a problem that can be solved quickly, neatly, or by one sector alone. The truth is that inequality in South Africa is structural, historical, psychological, and deeply embedded within the systems that shape our everyday lives. No single conference, organisation, government department, or industry can dismantle it on its own. What we can do, however, is contribute meaningfully to the work.

One of the most confronting things I have come to understand is that inequality is often reinforced by the things we no longer see. The hidden systems. The normalised behaviours. The everyday decisions we rarely question.

Growing up in South Africa, having what many families referred to as "an auntie" was completely normal. For many of us, these women helped raise us, cared for our homes, and became deeply woven into the fabric of family life. Yet very few of us stopped to ask why this form of labour became so normalised in South Africa in the first place. Only later did I begin to understand that this system of domestic labour was not accidental. It was structurally embedded through apartheid — a system designed to create cheap labour and economic dependency.

What felt ordinary in our homes was, in fact, connected to a much larger architecture of inequality. In many countries around the world, such labour is heavily protected and properly compensated. In South Africa, however, because inequality has become so deeply normalised, many of us perceive fair wages for domestic workers as "too expensive" or unrealistic. We rarely stop to interrogate why we think that way.

The same applies to many aspects of our daily lives. Where we buy our groceries. Which schools we send our children to. What coffee shops we sit in. What cars we aspire to drive. Which neighbourhoods we feel comfortable entering. Which businesses we trust. Who owns those businesses. Who benefits from our spending patterns.

These may appear to be ordinary lifestyle choices, but collectively they form part of what I have come to describe as the hidden or phantom enforcers of inequality — systems and behaviours so deeply embedded within our psyche that we no longer recognise them as structural drivers at all.

That is what has made this year's journey towards the conference so significant for me personally. What began as a conference has evolved into something far more reflective and intentional — a national classroom of ideas, accountability, interrogation, and imagination. We have come to understand that Corporate Social Investment cannot merely exist as project funding or annual compliance exercises. It must increasingly become part of a systems-based intervention that asks difficult questions about opportunity, access, dignity, employment, education, and the future of our country.

Beyond Bursaries: The Case for Corporate South Africa to Build Universities

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

8 minutes

Category

Education & CSI

As I reflected on the role of corporate social investment (CSI) in South Africa, one thought struck me: over the past 30 years, how much have we really built? How many schools, classrooms, laboratories, and libraries have been created through CSI, and what could we achieve if we shifted focus to universities — the institutions that prepare young South Africans to participate fully in the economy?

Let's start with the numbers. Corporate South Africa has consistently prioritised education in its CSI. In 2025, total CSI across all sectors was R13.1 billion, with education accounting for roughly 40%. Looking back from 1994 to 2025 — 32 years — cumulative CSI spend totals approximately R218 billion, of which around R87 billion was directed to education.

Historically, only 16% of education CSI went toward permanent infrastructure — schools, libraries, laboratories. That means R13.9 billion over 32 years has been spent on structural education projects. To put that into context, assume a fully equipped school costs around R20 million. Dividing the structural spend by the cost per school: 13,900 ÷ 20 = 695 schools.

So, over the past 32 years, CSI could have built approximately 695 fully equipped schools — classrooms, libraries, laboratories, and all. That is the tangible, lasting legacy of structural CSI spend, in contrast to the vast majority of funding (R73 billion) that went to programmatic initiatives such as bursaries, teacher development, and ICT support.

Now, let's pivot to the future. The CSI Indaba has a bold vision: over the next 30 years, corporate South Africa should focus on building three universities by 2055. These are not ordinary universities — each would require modern lecture halls, laboratories, libraries, student housing, research facilities, and digital infrastructure. Rough estimates suggest that constructing a single university of this scale could cost R10–15 billion, meaning three universities would require roughly R30–45 billion.

How can we get there? The structural spend that historically represented 16% of education CSI must increase to 30% by 2040. By making this shift, corporate CSI can move from reactive, programmatic impact to strategic, structural change. Simply put: if companies increase the proportion of their education budgets allocated to permanent infrastructure from 16% to 30%, they would have the resources to fund the construction of three universities over the next three decades.

To illustrate, consider Woolworths, which spent R52 million in cash CSI in 2024–2025 alongside R857 million in food donations. Feeding people is essential, yet a portion of these funds could be applied to building universities, creating a generational impact that far surpasses programmatic spending alone. Even a commitment of 10% of annual CSI cash spend toward this structural vision could accumulate significantly over decades.

The impact would be profound. Each university could enrol between 8,000 and 12,000 students per year, provide thousands of academic and administrative jobs, stimulate regional economies, and equip graduates with skills in science, technology, business, health, and the humanities. Research centres could foster innovation, incubators could support new enterprises, and graduates would enter the economy capable of creating value and reducing inequality.

Stellenbosch University, for example, receives over 100,000 applications for only 6,000 first-year places. The bottleneck is structural — insufficient lecture halls, laboratories, housing, and facilities. Redirecting CSI toward building universities addresses this challenge directly, moving South African CSI from reactive programme support to visionary, long-term infrastructure investment.

To recap the numbers:

  • Historical education CSI (1994–2025): R87 billion
  • Historical structural spend (16%): R13.9 billion → ~695 schools
  • Programmatic spend: R73 billion
  • Future structural target (30% by 2040) → enough to fund three universities by 2055
  • Estimated cost: R30–45 billion for three universities

This is the kind of transformational, generational CSI that the Indaba calls for: moving beyond temporary programmes to permanent, systemic impact. Feeding people today is essential, but building universities for tomorrow feeds minds and creates opportunity for generations.

Creating Value in the Social Era: Why the CSI Indaba Matters Now

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

CSI Strategy

I recently finished reading a fascinating book by Nilofer Merchant titled 11 Rules for Creating Value in the Social Era. The ideas in the book could not have come at a more appropriate moment for me. Over the past few weeks I have spent a great deal of time meeting with potential partners and clients to discuss the CSI Indaba, and during one of those meetings a client asked a simple but important question: what exactly is the value proposition of the CSI Indaba, and why should we partner with you rather than attend or support another platform in the sector?

It is a fair and necessary question. The Corporate Social Investment sector in South Africa already has several respected conferences and knowledge-sharing platforms. Many of these gatherings focus on reporting trends, research insights and case studies that showcase what companies are doing in their social investment portfolios. They provide valuable opportunities for networking, benchmarking and learning from the work of others. Yet the question that stayed with me after that meeting was not only how the CSI Indaba differs from those platforms, but also how we define value in the first place. The book by Nilofer Merchant helped crystallise this thinking.

Merchant argues that the way organisations create value changes as society evolves. In the Industrial Era, institutions were the primary engines of value creation. Organisations were designed like machines, structured into rigid departments such as engineering, manufacturing, finance and human resources. Success was measured by efficiency, scale and control. Later, as the digital revolution unfolded, the Information Age shifted the focus of value creation to data and knowledge. Organisations invested heavily in systems, reporting frameworks and information flows, allowing them to do the same things they had always done but with greater efficiency and speed.

Today, however, we have entered what Merchant calls the Social Era. In this era, value is created not simply by institutions or information, but by networks of connected individuals who collaborate, share ideas and organise around purpose.

One of the most striking elements of the book is that it opens with a symbolic obituary for what Merchant calls "traditional strategy". In this fictional obituary she notes that traditional strategy served organisations well for many decades but ultimately perished after colliding with the Social Era. The implication is not that strategy itself has died, but that the rigid, hierarchical models that once defined organisational success are increasingly unable to keep pace with a world shaped by connectivity, collaboration and fluid networks. Merchant makes a powerful observation: competition has changed, value propositions have changed, and work itself has changed, yet many organisations continue to operate with business models designed for a different time.

That insight helped me understand how to answer the question about the value proposition of the CSI Indaba. Most platforms in the sector focus on sharing what companies are already doing. They showcase corporate initiatives, highlight emerging trends and provide research that helps organisations refine their programmes. The CSI Indaba approaches the sector from a different starting point. Rather than asking how companies can improve existing initiatives, it asks a much larger question: how can Corporate Social Investment contribute to dismantling structural inequality in South Africa?

This question matters because South Africa remains one of the most unequal societies in the world. Addressing that inequality requires more than isolated programmes or annual reports. It requires long-term collaboration, systemic thinking and a national dialogue that extends far beyond a single event. The CSI Indaba has therefore been designed with a 25-year mandate rather than a yearly conference cycle. Its purpose is to create a sustained platform for conversation and action around the structural barriers that limit opportunity for millions of South Africans. These barriers include education, ownership, enterprise development, infrastructure and environmental sustainability. By focusing on these five structural constraints, the Indaba seeks to move the conversation from short-term projects to long-term transformation.

Woolworths and the CSI Illusion: What Are They Really Investing In?

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

7 minutes

Category

Corporate CSI

I was reviewing South Africa's top retailers and their corporate social investment (CSI) spend, and one question kept coming to mind: what is the actual impact of this investment? Take Woolworths Holdings Limited as an example. In the 2024–2025 financial year, Woolworths reported nearly R900 million in social impact. Yet, R857 million of that comprises surplus food donations — items approaching their sell-by date, redistributed to NGOs and food banks. The cash spent on community programmes? Just under R52 million, roughly 1% of net profit after tax, in line with standard CSI benchmarks.

Food donations are critical. Millions of South Africans face hunger daily, and redistributing unsold stock is both necessary and humane. But this is reactive impact, not visionary impact. What if Woolworths' R52 million cash CSI — the portion representing true investment — could be applied strategically and systemically, creating long-term solutions rather than addressing immediate needs alone?

Consider a bold vision. Suppose Woolworths committed 10% of its annual CSI cash spend towards the CSI Indaba's 30-year plan to build three universities. That would amount to roughly R5.2 million each year dedicated to this initiative. Over three decades, without any investment growth, the total would reach R156 million — a substantial contribution from a single company through annual budget allocation.

If other corporates joined in, these annual contributions could fund a meaningful portion of the capital required to construct three fully equipped universities, complete with lecture halls, laboratories, student housing, research centres, and digital infrastructure. Such universities could accommodate tens of thousands of students each year, addressing structural bottlenecks like those at Stellenbosch, where over 100 000 applicants compete for just 6 000 first-year places.

The potential impact is transformative. Each university could employ thousands of staff, stimulate regional economies, and provide skills training across science, technology, health, business, and the humanities. Over decades, this approach moves CSI from reactive programmes to visionary, systemic change.

The barriers to higher education in South Africa are structural — insufficient buildings, limited housing, and inadequate capacity — not a lack of talent or ambition. Redirecting CSI cash toward this challenge would expand access, empower regions, and build local economies, creating a system capable of preparing future generations for meaningful participation in the economy.

Woolworths already invests in education through scholarships, bursaries, and school programmes. Yet corporate South Africa must be held to a higher standard. Feeding people today is essential, but building institutions that serve generations is transformative.

The CSI Indaba 2026 theme, "The Inequality Mandate: Rewriting South Africa's Social Contract through Transformative Corporate Social Investment", calls for precisely this type of strategic thinking. It urges corporates to move from incremental programmes to systemic interventions, from reactive measures to visionary investments. Universities are one of the most powerful levers available — they reshape opportunity, address inequality at scale, and produce long-term societal returns.

The challenge to Woolworths and corporate leaders is clear: if you are already heavily invested in food security, why not apply the cash portion of your CSI to create permanent infrastructure for opportunity? Even a fraction of this spend could help build the next three universities over 30 years — a legacy that feeds not only the stomachs but also the minds of generations to come.

Join the conversation at the CSI Indaba 2026. Be part of the movement challenging corporates to think bigger, act boldly, and invest in the institutions that will define South Africa's future. Secure your ticket today and help shape a country where CSI builds universities, empowers communities, and creates lasting impact.

Rewriting South Africa's Corporate Social Investment: Women, Inequality, and the Mandate for Change

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

Women & Inequality

Inequality is not new to South Africa. It has been woven into the fabric of our society for generations, shaping who we are, what opportunities we have, and how power is distributed. For women, this inequality has often been compounded — a double burden of marginalisation in society at large and exclusion from decision-making spaces where wealth, influence, and opportunity are determined. Understanding the journey of women into South Africa's corporate and public sectors offers insight into the long-standing structures of inequality and the urgent need to challenge them today.

The legacy of women's activism in South Africa provides a powerful lens. In 1956, more than 20,000 women marched to the Union Buildings in Pretoria, protesting the pass laws that restricted the movement of black South Africans. This historic uprising was not only about resisting unjust legislation but also about claiming visibility, agency, and the right to participate fully in shaping society. It remains a defining moment in South Africa's struggle for equality, highlighting the courage and determination of women who demanded systemic change in a society built to silence them.

This month, as South Africa and the world celebrate International Women's Day, we reflect on how far women have come and how far we still need to go. The day serves as both a celebration of women's achievements and a reminder of persistent barriers in workplaces, government, and society. For many South African women, inclusion in the corporate mainstream remains limited, and gender disparities in leadership and remuneration continue to reflect structural inequality.

The inclusion of women in corporate and public spaces has been gradual and hard-won. After 1994, legislation such as the Employment Equity Act of 1998 and the Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) Codes sought to redress both gender and racial inequalities in the workplace. In public service, affirmative action and quotas increased women's representation in leadership roles, particularly in departments such as education, social development, and finance. These measures acknowledged that women's voices were crucial in shaping policies and programmes that affect millions of South Africans.

In the private sector, corporate inclusion has been slower. While diversity and inclusion policies are now commonplace, representation remains uneven, particularly for black women, who continue to face barriers in accessing senior leadership positions. Pay disparities and the undervaluation of women's contributions persist, demonstrating that inclusion on paper does not always translate into equity in practice. Yet, incremental progress is visible in leadership pipelines, mentorship programmes, and gender-responsive initiatives within forward-thinking organisations.

Inequality in South Africa is multi-layered, intersecting along lines of race, gender, class, and geography. It is a structural challenge that requires systemic solutions, not merely symbolic gestures. The CSI Indaba 2026 introduces an Inequality Mandate — a call to action for organisations to rethink how they invest in society, not only financially but strategically. This mandate challenges businesses to move beyond tokenistic representation and ensure that women, particularly black women, have meaningful influence in corporate decision-making, access to leadership pathways, and equitable remuneration.

The connection between the 1956 Women's March, International Women's Day, and today's corporate landscape is striking. The marchers fought to be seen and heard in a society designed to limit them; women in corporate spaces today continue to navigate structural barriers that echo past injustices. Just as the women of 1956 demanded systemic change, and International Women's Day celebrates and amplifies women's voices, the Inequality Mandate asks modern South African corporations to address inequality at its roots, embedding equity into every decision, investment, and strategic initiative.

Vision and Corporate Social Investment: Tackling Unemployment, Inequality, and Poverty in South Africa

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

7 minutes

Category

CSI Vision

In the evolving landscape of corporate governance, Corporate Social Investment (CSI) or Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has become a critical element for businesses aiming to contribute positively to society. In South Africa, where the legacies of unemployment, inequality, and poverty persist, the role of CSI must now be more than just particularly significant. This vision aims to amplify the integration of profitability with social good and address these entrenched socio-economic issues through collaborative efforts among CSI practitioners, NGOs, and the government.

The vision of Corporate Social Investment over the next 30 years should be to create a harmonious synergy between economic success and social development. This vision recognises that businesses have a dual responsibility: to generate financial returns for their shareholders and to contribute to the well-being of the communities in which they operate. In South Africa, this dual responsibility is crucial in the fight against unemployment, inequality, and poverty — three of the most pressing challenges (inherited from the last generation) facing the nation today.

Unemployment remains alarmingly high, with the official unemployment rate standing at approximately 33.9% as of 2023. Among the youth, this figure is even more stark, with nearly 60% of young people unemployed. The vision for CSI in this context involves creating sustainable employment opportunities through strategic investments in education, skills development, and entrepreneurship.

CSI initiatives focused on education and skills development can play a pivotal role in reducing unemployment. By investing in vocational training programmes, businesses can equip young people with the skills needed to enter the job market. Partnerships between corporates, NGOs, and educational institutions can help bridge the skills gap that currently hampers economic growth. For example, initiatives that support STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) education are essential. These programmes not only enhance employability but also foster innovation and economic diversification. By nurturing a skilled workforce, South African companies can contribute to reducing unemployment and driving economic growth.

Promoting entrepreneurship is key to creating livelihoods. I am sure we all know that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are the backbone of the economy, yet they often struggle to access funding and support. CSI practitioners must collaborate with NGOs and government agencies to create incubation hubs and provide seed funding.

By empowering entrepreneurs in rural and township areas to create their very own livelihoods, businesses can stimulate job creation and economic development at the grassroots level.

I am sure I do not have to repeat this but I will, South Africa remains one of the most unequal societies in the world, with a Gini coefficient of around 0.63. This stark inequality is not only a social injustice but also a barrier to sustainable economic growth. The vision for CSI must include initiatives that promote inclusivity and equal opportunities for all, irrespective of race, gender, or socio-economic background.

Inclusive growth requires deliberate efforts to ensure that economic benefits are widely shared. CSI initiatives must support marginalised communities by investing in local infrastructure, healthcare, and education. For instance, building clinics in underprivileged areas, funding scholarships for disadvantaged students, and supporting healthcare programmes can help level the playing field.

Within their own operations, businesses must lead by example by promoting diversity and inclusion. This involves creating equitable workplace policies, offering equal opportunities for advancement, and ensuring fair remuneration. By fostering an inclusive corporate culture, businesses can help reduce inequality and build a more just society.

Poverty affects nearly half of South Africa's population, with approximately 49.2% living below the national poverty line. Addressing poverty requires comprehensive and sustained efforts across multiple sectors. The vision for CSI involves a holistic approach that includes economic empowerment, social welfare, and sustainable development.

Aranda Textile Mills: Celebrating their Platinum Jubilee and Future Opportunities

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

5 minutes

Category

Corporate Stories

In the year 2023, Aranda Textile Mills celebrated 70 years in business. This notable milestone brought about a sense of reflection on the past and anticipation of what the future holds. Looking back to the early 1950s, South Africa saw the opening of what would become one of the country's leading manufacturers and suppliers of blankets, shawls and throws. Proprietors, the Magni family, had been active in the manufacture of textiles since the 1890's, from their factory in Prato, Italy, before relocating to South Africa after World War II.

Over the years, many developmental milestones and growth has taken place at Aranda. Today, the company is a fully-fledged vertical manufacturing plant and prides itself in offering a selection of the highest quality blankets, shawls and throws, ranging from classic to contemporary designs in an array of colours.

The Aranda product portfolio is diverse. It includes domestic, institutional, relief, church and traditional wearing blankets. They also manufacture a wide variety of shawls across many designs, colours and qualities, as well as a stunning range of contemporary décor throws and scatter cushions. The portfolio also includes in-house brands such as the Basotho Heritage Blankets, Haven & Earth, My Africa, as well as the Aranda Hotel Signature Collection.

Basotho Heritage Blankets have a deep cultural significance and history amongst Basotho people. They distinguish this nation from others by the way in which the blankets are worn as part of their everyday lives. Haven & Earth is a range of stylish and beautifully coordinated homeware. A new collection is launched every year, based on the latest global design and colour trends. The range is curated in such a way that the items can be mixed and matched to create layers of quiet luxury.

My Africa is a selection of bold and distinctive blankets and throws inspired by the many unique and diverse cultures and traditions found on the African continent. It celebrates the people who reside throughout these lands, who are bonded together through their deep-rooted heritage and African pride. Aranda also has the capability of manufacturing bespoke blankets and throws for chain stores and corporate companies. This capability has awarded Aranda the opportunity to manufacture products for many well-known companies, such as Woolworths, @ Home, Superbalist, Volpes and Pep, to name a few.

From the development and success of the Basotho Heritage Blankets brand, the Young Basotho Designers Collection was initiated. This initiative is aimed at empowering young designers of Basotho origin, by providing a platform for them to showcase their designs and tell Basotho stories through the medium of the blanket. The inaugural biennial collection was launched in 2022 and the second instalment earlier this year.

Similarly, as part of the My Africa brand, the Designer Collection aims to provide a platform for creatives to bring forth African-inspired cultural designs. By supporting Aranda, you are not only embracing quality but contributing to a responsible and proudly South African company. The future of Aranda is ensured by honouring the past while embracing the future.

Understanding Trauma in the Workplace and Its Impact on Corporate Social Investment

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

Workplace Wellness

Understanding trauma in the workplace is not just important; it is essential. Trauma can affect anyone, regardless of their role, background, or experience. It can stem from various sources, including personal experiences, workplace incidents, or broader societal events. When trauma is present in the workplace, it can have profound implications for employee well-being, productivity, and overall organisational culture.

Trauma is a response to a deeply distressing or disturbing event that overwhelms an individual's ability to cope. It can manifest in various ways, including emotional, psychological, and physical symptoms. In the workplace, trauma can result from incidents such as workplace violence, harassment, bullying, or even witnessing traumatic events. Additionally, employees may bring trauma from their personal lives into the workplace, affecting their ability to function effectively.

The impact of trauma in the workplace is multifaceted. Employees who have experienced trauma may struggle with concentration, memory, and decision-making. They may also experience increased anxiety, depression, or irritability, which can affect their relationships with colleagues and supervisors. Over time, these challenges can lead to decreased productivity, increased absenteeism, and higher turnover rates. Moreover, a workplace that does not address trauma can create a toxic environment, where employees feel unsupported and undervalued.

Corporate Social Investment (CSI) plays a crucial role in addressing trauma in the workplace. CSI initiatives can support employee mental health and well-being by funding counselling services, mental health awareness programmes, and trauma-informed training for managers and staff. By investing in these areas, organisations can create a supportive environment where employees feel safe to seek help and discuss their experiences.

Furthermore, CSI can extend beyond the workplace to support communities affected by trauma. For example, organisations can partner with NGOs that provide trauma counselling and support services to vulnerable populations. This not only benefits the community but also enhances the organisation's reputation as a socially responsible entity.

Creating a trauma-informed workplace requires a commitment from leadership to prioritise mental health and well-being. This involves implementing policies that support employees, such as flexible work arrangements, access to mental health resources, and regular training on trauma awareness. It also requires fostering a culture of empathy and understanding, where employees feel comfortable discussing their experiences without fear of stigma or discrimination.

Leadership plays a critical role in shaping workplace culture. When leaders demonstrate a genuine commitment to addressing trauma, it sets a tone for the entire organisation. This can be achieved through open communication, regular check-ins with employees, and modelling healthy work-life balance. By prioritising trauma-informed practices, leaders can create an environment where employees feel valued and supported.

Understanding trauma in the workplace is essential for creating a healthy, productive, and inclusive organisational culture. By investing in CSI initiatives that address trauma, organisations can support their employees and communities, ultimately contributing to a more resilient and compassionate society. The time to act is now — let us commit to creating workplaces where trauma is understood, addressed, and transformed into opportunities for growth and healing.

For three decades, Absa has demonstrated an unwavering commitment to community empowerment through its corporate citizenship initiatives. The bank's journey in corporate social investment (CSI) reflects a deep understanding of its role in society and a strategic approach to creating lasting impact across the African continent.

Absa's corporate citizenship journey began long before CSI became a formal requirement for businesses. From its early days, the bank recognised that its success was intrinsically linked to the well-being of the communities it served. This realisation laid the foundation for what would become one of South Africa's most comprehensive and impactful CSI programmes.

Over the years, Absa's CSI strategy has evolved to address the changing needs of society while maintaining a focus on sustainable development. The bank's approach is guided by strategic intent, ensuring that every initiative is designed to create measurable impact and contribute to long-term social transformation.

One of the hallmarks of Absa's corporate citizenship is its focus on education. The bank has invested significantly in educational programmes, from early childhood development to tertiary education support. These investments have enabled thousands of young South Africans to access quality education and develop the skills needed to participate meaningfully in the economy.

Beyond education, Absa has made substantial contributions to enterprise development. By supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the bank has helped create jobs and stimulate economic growth in communities that need it most. These initiatives include funding, mentorship, and capacity-building programmes designed to help entrepreneurs thrive.

Absa's commitment to community empowerment extends to health and social welfare. The bank has supported numerous health initiatives, including HIV/AIDS programmes, maternal and child health projects, and access to healthcare for underserved communities. These efforts have improved health outcomes and enhanced the quality of life for countless individuals.

The bank's environmental sustainability initiatives reflect its understanding of the interconnectedness of social and environmental challenges. Absa has implemented programmes to promote sustainable agriculture, water conservation, and renewable energy, contributing to environmental protection while creating economic opportunities for communities.

As Absa marks 30 years of corporate citizenship, it continues to innovate and adapt its CSI strategy to meet emerging challenges. The bank's commitment to community empowerment remains as strong as ever, guided by the belief that businesses have a responsibility to contribute positively to society.

The evolution of Absa's corporate citizenship serves as an inspiring example of how strategic, long-term investment in communities can create transformative impact. As the bank looks to the future, its commitment to community empowerment will undoubtedly continue to shape lives and contribute to a more equitable and prosperous Africa.

What to Do When You Feel Overwhelmed: A Practical Guide

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

5 minutes

Category

Personal Development

Feeling overwhelmed is something almost everyone experiences at some point. Whether it's due to work, personal challenges, or the general demands of life, that sense of being buried under too much to handle can be paralyzing. The good news is that there are practical steps you can take to regain control and move forward.

The first step when you feel overwhelmed is to pause and acknowledge what you're feeling. It's okay to admit that you're struggling. Taking a moment to breathe and recognise your emotions can help prevent the feeling from escalating. This pause gives you the space to assess the situation more clearly.

Once you've paused, the next step is to break down whatever is overwhelming you into smaller, manageable tasks. When everything feels like one giant mountain, it's easy to feel defeated. By breaking it down into smaller hills, you can tackle one thing at a time. This approach not only makes the work seem less daunting but also gives you a sense of progress as you complete each task.

Prioritisation is key. Not everything needs to be done immediately. Identify what is truly urgent and what can wait. Focus on the most important tasks first and give yourself permission to let go of the rest for now. This doesn't mean ignoring responsibilities, but rather being strategic about where you direct your energy.

Don't be afraid to ask for help. Whether it's delegating tasks at work, seeking support from friends and family, or even speaking to a professional, reaching out can make a significant difference. You don't have to carry everything on your own. Sharing the load can provide relief and new perspectives.

Taking care of your physical and mental well-being is crucial when you're feeling overwhelmed. Ensure you're getting enough sleep, eating well, and engaging in some form of physical activity. These basic self-care practices can have a profound impact on your ability to cope with stress.

Finally, remember to be kind to yourself. Feeling overwhelmed doesn't mean you're weak or incapable. It means you're human. Treat yourself with the same compassion you would offer a friend in a similar situation. This self-compassion can help you bounce back more quickly.

Overwhelming feelings are temporary. By taking practical steps to manage them, you can regain your sense of control and move forward with confidence. Remember, you've faced challenges before, and you have the strength to overcome this one too.

The Future Of Corporate Social Investment: Insights From Lunga Schoeman – Head Of CSI – DBSA

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

Leadership Insights

In the latest episode of The Future of Corporate Social Investment (CSI), Lunga Schoeman, a veteran in the field of corporate social responsibility, shares his insights on the evolving landscape of CSI and what the future might hold. As the Head of CSI at the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA), Lunga brings a wealth of experience and a unique perspective on how CSI can drive sustainable development.

Lunga's journey in CSI spans over two decades, during which he has witnessed significant shifts in how businesses approach social investment. According to Lunga, the early days of CSI were characterised by philanthropic gestures — businesses giving back to communities without necessarily measuring impact or aligning with strategic objectives. Today, the landscape has transformed dramatically, with CSI becoming an integral part of corporate strategy and governance.

One of the key trends Lunga identifies is the move towards impact investing. Unlike traditional CSI, which often focused on charitable giving, impact investing seeks to generate measurable social and environmental impact alongside financial returns. This shift reflects a growing recognition that businesses can create shared value — benefiting both society and their bottom line.

Another important development is the emphasis on data and measurement. Lunga emphasises that the future of CSI will be data-driven, with organisations increasingly using metrics to assess the effectiveness of their initiatives. This approach not only ensures accountability but also enables continuous improvement and more strategic allocation of resources.

Collaboration is also emerging as a critical theme. Lunga notes that the complex challenges facing society cannot be solved by any single organisation. Instead, partnerships between the public sector, private sector, and civil society are essential for creating meaningful and sustainable impact. The DBSA, under Lunga's leadership, has been at the forefront of fostering such collaborations.

Looking ahead, Lunga believes that technology will play an increasingly important role in CSI. From digital platforms that facilitate transparency to innovative solutions that address social challenges, technology has the potential to amplify the impact of CSI initiatives. However, he cautions that technology must be deployed thoughtfully, with a focus on inclusivity and accessibility.

Lunga's insights offer a compelling vision for the future of CSI — one that is strategic, collaborative, and impact-oriented. As businesses continue to navigate this evolving landscape, his experience and wisdom serve as invaluable guides for those seeking to make a meaningful difference through corporate social investment.

The Power of Collaboration in South Africa's NGO Sector: A Perspective from Julia Sotirianakos

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

NGO Sector

South Africa's non-governmental organisation (NGO) sector is a vast and intricate landscape, teeming with passionate individuals and groups dedicated to making a difference. From grassroots community initiatives to large-scale national organisations, NGOs play a critical role in addressing social challenges and driving positive change.

Julia Sotirianakos, a seasoned professional with deep experience in the NGO sector, offers valuable insights into the power of collaboration. According to Julia, the challenges facing South Africa are too complex for any single organisation to address alone. Collaboration is not just beneficial — it's essential.

One of the key benefits of collaboration is resource optimisation. NGOs often operate with limited resources, and by working together, they can pool their expertise, funding, and networks to achieve greater impact. This approach reduces duplication of efforts and ensures that resources are directed where they are needed most.

Collaboration also enables knowledge sharing. Each NGO brings unique experiences, perspectives, and solutions to the table. By sharing this knowledge, organisations can learn from each other's successes and failures, leading to more effective and innovative approaches to addressing social challenges.

Julia emphasises that collaboration should extend beyond the NGO sector to include partnerships with government and the private sector. These cross-sector partnerships can leverage the strengths of each stakeholder — the scale and resources of government, the innovation and agility of the private sector, and the grassroots knowledge and community trust of NGOs.

However, collaboration is not without its challenges. Julia notes that building effective partnerships requires trust, clear communication, and aligned objectives. It also requires a willingness to share credit and recognition, which can be difficult in a sector where funding and visibility are often tied to individual organisational achievements.

Despite these challenges, the potential benefits of collaboration far outweigh the obstacles. Julia has witnessed numerous successful collaborations that have transformed communities and created lasting impact. These examples serve as inspiration for what can be achieved when organisations work together towards a common goal.

Looking ahead, Julia believes that collaboration will become increasingly important as South Africa continues to navigate complex social and economic challenges. The NGO sector must continue to foster a culture of collaboration, both within the sector and with external partners, to maximise its collective impact.

Julia Sotirianakos's perspective offers a compelling case for the power of collaboration in South Africa's NGO sector. Her insights remind us that while individual organisations can make a difference, it is through working together that we can create transformative and sustainable change.
