30 Years of Democracy in South Africa: Reflections, Challenges, and the Path Forward

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

January 2025

Reading Time

7 minutes

Category

National Reflection

Thirty years ago, South Africa emerged from the darkness of apartheid into the light of democracy. The transition was a moment of profound hope and optimism, marked by the first democratic elections and the inauguration of Nelson Mandela as the country's first black president. As we reflect on three decades of democracy, it is essential to acknowledge both the progress made and the challenges that remain.

The achievements of the past 30 years are significant. South Africa has built a robust constitutional democracy, with one of the most progressive constitutions in the world. The Bill of Rights guarantees fundamental freedoms and protections for all citizens, regardless of race, gender, or sexual orientation. This legal framework has been instrumental in advancing human rights and social justice.

Access to basic services has improved dramatically. Millions of South Africans now have access to clean water, electricity, and housing — services that were denied to the majority under apartheid. The expansion of social grants has provided a critical safety net for vulnerable populations, reducing poverty and improving quality of life for many.

Education has also seen significant expansion. More children are attending school, and higher education institutions have opened their doors to a more diverse student body. These investments in human capital are essential for building a skilled workforce capable of driving economic growth and development.

However, the challenges facing South Africa are equally significant. Unemployment remains stubbornly high, particularly among young people. Inequality continues to plague the country, with the gap between rich and poor remaining one of the highest in the world. These structural issues are a legacy of apartheid and require sustained, strategic intervention.

Corruption has undermined public trust and diverted resources away from critical services. The state capture era revealed the extent to which democratic institutions can be compromised, eroding the foundations of good governance. Rebuilding trust and strengthening institutions is a priority for the future.

Service delivery protests reflect the frustration of communities that feel left behind. While progress has been made, the pace of change has not met expectations in many areas. Addressing these disparities requires a renewed commitment to inclusive development and equitable distribution of resources.

Looking ahead, the path forward requires collective effort. Government, business, civil society, and citizens must work together to address the challenges facing the country. Corporate Social Investment has a critical role to play in this collective effort, supporting initiatives that create jobs, build skills, and foster inclusive growth.

The next 30 years of democracy must be characterised by renewed energy and commitment to the ideals that inspired the transition. This includes strengthening democratic institutions, combating corruption, and ensuring that the benefits of economic growth are shared by all South Africans.

Thirty years of democracy is a milestone worth celebrating, but also a moment for honest reflection. South Africa has come a long way, but the journey is far from complete. By learning from the past and committing to a shared vision for the future, South Africa can build on its achievements and create a more just, equitable, and prosperous society for all.

CSI Legacy Awards 2026 Honours South Africa's Leading Social Impact Champions

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

July 2026

Reading Time

5 minutes

Category

Awards

Johannesburg, South Africa – 17 July 2026 – South Africa's corporate social investment community gathered at 22 On Sloane in Johannesburg on 16 July 2026 for the fifth annual CSI Legacy Awards, celebrating eight outstanding organisations and leaders whose work continues to create meaningful and lasting change across the country.

Held as the closing celebration of the inaugural CSI Indaba, the CSI Legacy Awards brought together leaders from business, civil society, academia and the development sector. The event was completely sold out, with additional seats brought into the venue to accommodate more guests and fill the room.

The extraordinary turnout reflected the growing stature of the CSI Legacy Awards and the sector's commitment to recognising organisations and individuals who are moving beyond charitable interventions towards sustainable, systemic and community-led change.

PinkDrive, led by founder and Chief Executive Officer Noelene Kotschan, received the award for Best NGO. The organisation was recognised for its continued commitment to improving access to cancer education, early detection and healthcare services, particularly among communities that remain underserved by South Africa's healthcare system.

The Best Woman in CSI award was presented to Juanita Pardesi of the Seriti Institute. Pardesi was honoured for her leadership, dedication and contribution to building stronger communities through inclusive and purpose-driven development.

Family Life Centre, represented by Jennifer Papers, was named Best Rising NGO. The award recognises an emerging organisation demonstrating significant potential, strong community relevance and a growing ability to respond to the social challenges facing families and communities.

Martin Sweet of Primestars South Africa received the Best CEO award. Sweet was recognised for leadership that has consistently placed young people, education and economic opportunity at the centre of business purpose.

PETCO, represented by Samu Mkhize, was awarded Best Green Impact for its contribution to environmental sustainability, recycling and the advancement of a circular economy.

UR Global, represented by Luleka Mkhuzo, received the award for Best Rural Community Project. The organisation was recognised for its commitment to bringing meaningful development opportunities to rural communities.

The Best Corporate award went to Oceana Group, represented by Zodwa Velleman. The award acknowledges the company's commitment to responsible corporate citizenship and its investment in programmes that contribute to social development, food security and stronger communities.

Taking Care of Business, represented by Tracey Chambers, was named Best Social Enterprise. The organisation was recognised for combining an entrepreneurial model with a clear social mission, creating pathways to economic participation, dignity and independence.

The 2026 CSI Legacy Awards formed part of a broader week of reflection and action hosted through the CSI Indaba, under the theme: "The Inequality Mandate: Rewriting South Africa's Social Contract through Transformative Corporate Social Investment."

When Bringing It In-House Isn't Enough: Lessons from FirstRand Foundation

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

June 2026

Reading Time

7 minutes

Category

CSI Strategy

Every time I return home in rural Mpumalanga, Kabokweni, for the holidays, I am reminded that some of South Africa's most important development lessons are hidden in plain sight. They are not found in boardrooms, strategy documents or annual reports. They are found in the everyday realities of ordinary people and in the communities that have quietly endured decades of economic change, political transition and development intervention.

One of the first things I notice whenever I return is a gogo who sells tomatoes outside the local hospital. She has been there for as long as I can remember. Through changing governments, economic downturns, rising food prices and countless development initiatives, she has remained a constant presence. Every morning she arrives with stock. Every day she serves her customers. Every evening she packs up and returns the next day to do it all again.

What fascinates me is not that she sells fruit and vegetables. What fascinates me is that she has managed to remain relevant for years. Hospitals are ecosystems. Patients arrive. Families visit loved ones. Nurses begin and end their shifts. Taxi drivers wait for passengers. Through experience and observation, this gogo recognised an opportunity. She positioned herself where people needed her and built a business around a consistent flow of demand.

The more I reflect on her story, the more I realise that sustainability is not something she talks about—it is something she lives. Without consultants, strategy documents or impact reports, she has built a small enterprise that has survived where many funded initiatives have come and gone.

Years ago, large parts of downtown Johannesburg were regarded as symbols of urban decline. Buildings stood empty. Investment had disappeared. Yet Jonathan Liebmann looked at those same buildings and saw something different. He saw possibility. He saw value where others saw neglect. The result was Maboneng. Maboneng was not created through another bursary programme or another awareness campaign. It was built through vision. It emerged because somebody looked at neglected assets and imagined a different future.

A few years ago, FirstRand Foundation announced that it would bring its social investment portfolio in-house, ending its long-standing relationship with Tshikululu Social Investments. At the time, many people within the sector viewed the decision as a bold strategic move. The foundation appeared to be creating an opportunity for greater control, greater alignment and perhaps most importantly, greater innovation.

Those are not small questions. In fact, I would argue that they are the most important questions any foundation can ask. What is failing in our communities? What interventions have already been tried repeatedly? Which programmes are oversaturated? What assets already exist that could be repurposed? How do we create sustainable economic ecosystems rather than temporary interventions?

South Africa does not suffer from a shortage of literacy programmes, bursary schemes or educational interventions. These are among the most heavily funded areas within the CSI sector. Yet despite these investments, many communities continue to struggle with unemployment, economic exclusion and declining local economies. Perhaps the challenge is not a lack of funding. Perhaps the challenge is a lack of imagination.

Imagine if FirstRand Foundation had used its strategic independence to identify struggling towns across South Africa and commit itself to economic regeneration. Imagine if abandoned cinemas were transformed into centres of excellence for Technical and Vocational Education and Training. Imagine if old emafemini were converted into manufacturing hubs, entrepreneurial incubators, digital innovation centres or community-owned enterprises.

The lesson of FirstRand Foundation's move in-house is that strategic independence means very little without strategic imagination. South Africa does not need another generation of programmes that simply manage social challenges. It needs institutions willing to reimagine local economies, repurpose forgotten assets and build ecosystems of opportunity.

What the Silence of CSI Amid South Africa's Xenophobic Tensions Reveals About Its Impact on Communities

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

June 2026

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

Editor's View

Last week, during a private CSI Indaba Build-Up Session, clinical psychologist and organisational development specialist Nomfundo Mogapi shared a metaphor that has remained with me ever since. Using the image of a tree, she argued that Corporate Social Investment has become exceptionally good at funding what is visible. We fund the tree trunk, the branches and the leaves. These are the programmes, projects, outputs, targets, reports and beneficiary numbers that dominate annual CSI reports and sustainability presentations.

Yet beneath every healthy tree lies something equally important: the roots and the soil. The roots represent trust, dignity, leadership, relationships, belonging and social cohesion. The soil represents the environment in which communities live and programmes operate — conditions shaped by inequality, exclusion, unemployment, historical trauma and social fragmentation.

As South Africa once again grapples with xenophobic tensions, growing frustration around immigration and troubling scenes of communities turning against one another, her question feels more relevant than ever. Perhaps the issue is not simply why Corporate Social Investment appears largely absent from this conversation. Perhaps the more important question is whether moments like these reveal something about the depth of CSI's impact on the communities it has spent the last three decades trying to strengthen.

For more than 30 years, Corporate Social Investment has positioned itself as one of South Africa's most important mechanisms for social development. Billions of rand have been invested into education, youth development, food security, entrepreneurship, health and community upliftment. Yet when social tensions emerge and communities begin to fracture, the sector often finds itself with very little to say.

The true measure of community development is not how communities function when conditions are favourable. The true measure is how they respond when pressure arrives. It is how communities behave when unemployment rises, when resources become scarce, when frustration grows, when uncertainty takes hold and when people begin searching for someone to blame.

Xenophobia emerges when economically vulnerable people begin competing with other economically vulnerable people for limited opportunities. It emerges when communities feel abandoned and disconnected from opportunity. It emerges when frustration seeks a target and when social cohesion weakens under pressure.

This does not excuse xenophobic behaviour. But it does require us to understand it. And if xenophobia is one of the symptoms of inequality, then surely it deserves greater attention from a sector whose purpose is to address social development and help build stronger communities.

Perhaps what these tensions reveal is that CSI has become exceptionally effective at funding interventions but less effective at understanding systems. We count the number of bursaries awarded. We measure the number of young people trained. We track the number of meals distributed. But do we measure trust? Do we measure belonging? Do we measure social cohesion?

When communities fracture, when fear overtakes solidarity and when vulnerable people turn against one another, we are witnessing more than a policy failure or an economic failure. We may be witnessing the moment when the roots are tested. And perhaps the silence of CSI amidst South Africa's xenophobic tensions tells us less about what the sector thinks and more about what it has — or has not — succeeded in building.

Stellenbosch University Denies Thousands of Black Learners: Is Race or Capacity the Real Barrier?

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

February 2026

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

CSI Insight

I was listening to the radio this past week when a parent was complaining that their child had not been accepted into Stellenbosch University because they believed their child was black. At first, I was drawn into the emotion of the story — the disappointment, the frustration, the very human reaction to a system that seems to exclude. But upon further reflection, I realised the issue is not as simple as skin colour.

Stellenbosch University receives over 106,000 applications for only 6,000 first-year places. By any stretch of the imagination, it is impossible for such a large number of applicants to be accommodated. The bottleneck is structural, not personal, and it is here that corporate South Africa must step up through corporate social investment (CSI).

The thought led me to consider the potential of CSI to address higher education access at scale. For decades, CSI has invested in schools, clinics, libraries, skills programmes and community development projects. These efforts are vital, but they rarely tackle the structural inequalities that persist across our economy. If CSI could fund the building of thousands of schools, why could it not also invest in building universities — the very institutions that prepare our young people for meaningful participation in the economy?

If over the next 30 years, CSI were to build three top-tier universities, it could help to create a system capable of accommodating tens of thousands of students who would otherwise be left behind. Each new university could enrol between 8,000 and 12,000 students per year, meaning three universities could provide access to roughly 30,000 new places annually.

The cost of such universities is significant but within reach. A modern, research-focused university could require R10–R15 billion in phased development. Building three universities could total R30–R45 billion over 30 years. Beyond financial expenditure, the projects would create jobs at multiple levels — from construction workers, architects, and engineers during the building phase to professors, lecturers, administrative staff, and support roles during operations.

Location would be a key factor to ensure accessibility and impact. In the Eastern Cape, a university could serve students from historically under-served rural and peri-urban areas. In Mpumalanga or Limpopo, universities could help address skills gaps in agriculture, mining, and technology sectors. A third university in the Northern Cape could provide opportunities for remote communities.

This vision aligns directly with the CSI Indaba's 2026 theme: "The Inequality Mandate: Rewriting South Africa's Social Contract through Transformative Corporate Social Investment." Universities are one of the most powerful levers available. They transform lives, empower communities, and provide the long-term infrastructure required to dismantle structural barriers.

The question for leaders at the CSI Indaba is clear: are we prepared to invest boldly, act strategically, and create systemic change? The next generation of South Africans should not be counted among the 100,000+ who cannot access a university place. The time to build universities that can serve them is now, and CSI South Africa has the power to lead the way.

CSI South Africa: 30 Years of CSI Spend Almost Equivalent to Eswatini and Lesotho GDP Combined

Simphiwe Mtetwa

Published

February 2026

Reading Time

6 minutes

Category

CSI Insight

I was reading a book by Salim Ismail, Exponential Organizations, and in it he recounts a striking anecdote about Motorola's Iridium satellite project. The company invested billions of dollars and assembled some of the brightest minds in the world, yet the project failed spectacularly. One of the key reasons? Motorola assumed customers would pay around $3,000 for a single satellite phone. That one assumption, more than any technical flaw, ultimately sank the project.

This story resonates powerfully with South Africa's corporate social investment (CSI) sector. Over the past 30 years, corporate South Africa has poured roughly R123 billion into social development initiatives — funding meant to build schools, clinics, roads, and communities. That amount is nearly equivalent to the combined GDP of Eswatini and Lesotho.

Yet, despite this staggering investment, South Africa remains the most unequal country on planet earth. Millions of people continue to live in grinding poverty, trapped by structural barriers and systemic inefficiencies. Billions of rands have been spent on programmes, projects, and campaigns — yet the social fabric remains fractured.

The uncomfortable question arises: what have we actually been funding? For decades, CSI initiatives have targeted development, but often in piecemeal ways. Education programmes, skills development, and small infrastructure projects — all valuable in isolation — have rarely addressed the systemic constraints that prevent meaningful change.

The lesson from Motorola's Iridium project is instructive: even brilliant ideas and vast resources can fail if underlying assumptions about context, demand, or execution are flawed. CSI spend, no matter how large, cannot achieve transformation if it does not account for the scale, interconnections, and realities of the problems it seeks to solve.

This is why the CSI Indaba 2026 is more important than ever. The event takes on the theme: "The Inequality Mandate: Rewriting South Africa's Social Contract through Transformative Corporate Social Investment." It is not about optics or incrementalism; it is about confronting decades of underwhelming outcomes and asking the hard questions: what must we fund, why must we fund it, and how will it lead to measurable, systemic transformation?

These binding constraints include: Education and skills gaps — enabling citizens to fully participate in the economy. Inequitable access to assets — from land to capital, opening doors for sustainable livelihoods. Market barriers for small businesses — empowering entrepreneurship and local economies. Infrastructure disparities — connecting communities to essential services. Climate vulnerability — mitigating risks for the most exposed populations.

South Africa cannot afford another thirty years of miscalculation. The stakes are too high. We have the resources. We have the knowledge. We have the technology. Failure is not an option when millions of lives are affected by structural inequities that billions of rands were meant to address.

The CSI Indaba is just the beginning. The real work starts within each of us. It is a call to courage, reflection, and disciplined action. Because in South Africa, the lesson is clear: resources alone are not enough. Insight, precision, and systemic vision are what will truly transform our country.

Our History

From CSR News to a 30-year vision for African impact.

Simphiwe Mtetwa began with a simple purpose: report the stories, research and decisions shaping South Africa's CSI sector, then turn that knowledge into action for companies, communities and changemakers.

Explore The Journey Visit CSI Indaba 2026
A South African company with a global feel

Connecting decision-makers to change-makers.

What started as a focused CSI news platform has grown into a strategic publishing, research and convening company serving corporate leaders, government, NGOs, academics and social-impact practitioners across the continent.

4,000+ Industry subscribers reached through CSI news, insight and thought leadership.
50+ Decision-makers connected through research, campaigns and sector conversations.
R7B+ Combined client and partner budgets represented across development work.
2052 A long-term vision guiding measurable targets and community investment.
The Journey

Built from reporting, sharpened by strategy, expanded through convening.

01

A focused CSI newsroom

The work began as CSR News, created to report on corporate social responsibility and help the sector see where money, need and opportunity were moving.

02

A trusted sector platform

The platform grew into a home for development news, interviews, research and practical insight for leaders responsible for corporate giving and social investment.

03

The Simphiwe Mtetwa chapter

The company evolved into Simphiwe Mtetwa (Pty) Ltd, carrying the founder-led reputation into a broader strategy, publishing, events and advisory platform.

04

South Africa's biggest CSI classroom

CSI Indaba 2026 became a major milestone, bringing corporate leaders and changemakers together to confront inequality, systems change and the future of CSI.

Leadership And Community

Inspired knowledge inspires action.

Across its work, Simphiwe Mtetwa has stayed close to one belief: CSI should not be random giving. It should be clear, measurable, connected to communities and brave enough to build what remains after funding ends.

The company works alongside government, corporate leaders, authors, academics, NGOs and development practitioners to help the sector move from good intentions to stronger systems.

What the work now includes

  • CSI research, reports and strategic storytelling
  • Digital publishing and sector news platforms
  • Enterprise development and community campaigns
  • Events, awards and high-level impact conversations
The GivenGroup Foundation

A business guided by a 30-year vision of building better communities.

Part of the Simphiwe Mtetwa story is a long-term commitment to give back through The GivenGroup Foundation, linking the company's publishing, research and convening work to practical community development.

Developing A Thriving Vision Building Better Communities

Giving is treated here as part of the work itself: generous, intentional, community-centred and connected to what South Africa needs now.

Explore Our Work Get In Touch
Overview

Who we are.
Why we exist.

Connecting decision-makers to change-makers.

We are South Africa's fastest-growing corporate social responsibility news platform, with the specific goal of helping South African corporate decision-makers define and develop corporate giving.

We have over 3,422 industry subscribers, around 42 of whom are decision-makers, with a combined budget of over ZAR 5 billion (USD 330 million). We work alongside government, captains of industry, inspired authors, academics and industry enthusiasts to champion real change in South African social development.

Clients trust our CSI expertise, which we combine with cutting edge research and high-level skills in digital innovation. Our work enables the South African CSI industry to deliver impact better, faster and with more enduring outcomes.

Our 30-year vision and 10-year commitment to give 10% of our profits to communities through The GivenGroup Foundation give us the ability to impact more communities through two strong business models: the business and the foundation.

What We Do

Three functions, delivered as one system.

Turning social investment ambition into meaningful action.

We create content on social responsibility, helping government, corporates, consultants, NPOs and NGOs to reach their target markets through appropriate, targeted development news. We work with modern and ambitious clients who want to define the future through delivering quality programmes and projects that impact the 'body, mind and soul' of the communities in which they work.

Captains of industry rely on us to solve industry-defining challenges in strategy, digital transformation, research, content development, creative design and enterprise development, all with a strong social responsibility component.

We measure our success by the success of our clients and partners, driven by a passion to see corporate social responsibility done better. Our years of experience in the sector enables clients to develop a clearer vision, a more informed strategy and better, more detail-oriented implementation. We follow this up by co-writing, editing and designing attractive and impactful CSI reports that capture what you have achieved.

Explore What We Do
Our People

Experience across business, communities and social investment.

Simphiwe Mtetwa operates as a well-oiled machine informed by a strong set of entrepreneurial beliefs and values. Our team members, experts in their fields, are celebrated, valued, and encouraged to bring their full, authentic selves to the workplace. The result is a stimulating work environment where team members challenge each other constantly—questioning, posing alternatives, and constantly pushing boundaries for the best possible solution for our clients.

Our team includes academics, MBA students, masters graduates and a strong cohort of journalists and editors. Each of us plays our part in ensuring that projects are executed with flair and precision. We take considerable care in recruiting and skilling our teams, regardless of their already high levels of competence when they join.

Meet The Team
What We Believe

Sustainable change begins with listening.

Our passion is to do good, resting upon a strong foundation of Christian values and beliefs. Although not all staff members are Christian, the faith of the Simphiwe Mtetwa and core team carries the vision forward, informing how we relate to our clients and communities. Projects are executed with integrity and communication is transparent. If we don't know something, we ask. If we think a client can do better, we say so. We strive to execute projects boldly, but in a spirit of constant learning.

We love creativity and innovation, combining it with discipline and hard data—always a winning combination when a team gets it right. We're aware, too, that while faith is constant, the context in which we work is always changing and that only by changing tactics, methodologies and skills will we stay abreast of the complex realities of a country like South Africa.

Our beliefs, in a nutshell?

01

Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and all your strength, and

02

Love your neighbour as yourself.'

The Invisible Drivers of Inequality

The Invisible Architecture of Inequality: Trauma, Power, and the Limits of Corporate Social Investment

This session challenges participants to confront what is often left unseen: how trauma, power, and history shape decisions ? and ultimately, outcomes ? we fail to achieve. It examines why well-intentioned social investment has not sufficiently reduced inequality.

  • Insight into the psychological and systemic forces influencing CSI decisions

  • Trauma, power and historical influence on corporate social investment
  • Rethinking how corporate social investment creates meaningful change
